news.title: Why Canada needs to develop the Superpower capacity to defeat a U.S. military attack : The Canadian Business Daily
news.text:
To avoid being reduced to an economic vassal state, Ottawa must abandon the comfort of the American umbrella, embrace decentralized deterrence, and ground national security in community health and Indigenous territorial sovereignty.

For generations, the cornerstone of Canadian foreign policy was an unwritten pact of proximity: Washington provided the continental shield, Ottawa maintained a modest conventional force, and both capitals operated within a predictable architecture of shared democratic norms. That architecture has collapsed. In an era dominated by hyper-nationalist rhetoric, trade ultimatums, and casual musings about northern annexation, Canada must confront an existential reality. Economic sovereignty cannot survive without credible hard power. If Ottawa cannot establish the physical leverage to defend its own territory, Canadian negotiators will inevitably be reduced to what Mark Carney has warned is the permanent subservience of a "vassal state".

Power respects power. A transactional Washington does not adjust its posture out of deference to international law or nostalgic sentiment; it calculates risks, costs, and counterweights. To establish an unyielding deterrent, Canada must break with outdated binational dependencies and construct a comprehensive, six-layer total-defence web—a decentralized force of roughly one million organized defenders.

Central to this structural transformation is the Indigenous Sovereign Shield, an operational layer that bridges territorial defence with long-overdue restorative justice. Modern deterrence cannot be achieved through top-down mandates from Ottawa alone. By recognizing and equipping First Nations, Inuit, and Métis communities to exercise their inherent rights across their traditional lands, Canada activates an incomparable tactical advantage: generational knowledge of terrain, waterways, and Arctic corridors capable of denying an aggressor mobility through asymmetric attrition.

Crucially, this indigenous defence layer links operational preparedness directly to comprehensive community resilience. Military readiness is impossible in regions burdened by chronic underfunding, housing instability, or inadequate public health infrastructure. The Indigenous Sovereign Shield establishes integrated healthcare, trauma-informed care networks, and local food and water security protocols as primary pillars of national defence. In this framework, building modern medical facilities, training local medical responders, and ensuring community well-being are not merely social policies—they are the vital, non-negotiable requirements of an unbroken territorial defence.

I. The Illusion of the Shield

The global geopolitical landscape has fundamentally shifted, and with it, Canada’s longest-held security assumption has shattered. For over a century, Canadian defence policy rested on a comfortable premise: that our geographic proximity to the United States was our ultimate shield, and that our shared democratic values guaranteed our sovereignty. But we are no longer living in that world. In the current era of a transactional, hyper-nationalistic Washington, Ottawa must confront an uncomfortable, seemingly radical truth: Canada must develop a formidable military capability, not only to defend itself from a physical invasion, but to secure the basic leverage required to negotiate trade deals that do not reduce us to the status of a permanent economic protectorate.

To many, the notion of a U.S. military threat sounds like far-fetched fiction, the stuff of late-night alternative history forums. But as analysts at The Conversation observe, the risk of asymmetric coercion is no longer purely hypothetical. As the Trump administration actively deploys "MAGA" propaganda to condition the American electorate for an annexation of Canada "out of necessity"—even circulating disturbing maps depicting Canada as a conquered 51st state—the geopolitical reality demands cold-blooded realism.

These information campaigns mimic classical, dangerous 20th-century pre-war psychological conditioning, attempting to frame a peaceful neighbour as an adversary to lower the domestic barrier to aggression. Boundaries, trade agreements, and territorial sovereignty are no longer sacrosanct to an American political class that increasingly views foreign policy through a lens of raw leverage. Security dependency breeds political servitude; without hard power, our economic autonomy is an illusion.

The core lesson of this brave new world has been laid bare by Washington’s interactions with Beijing. China has effectively proven that modern America is no longer a society that leads from a sense of moral superiority or an enlightened system of values. The days of the United States acting as the principled "leader of the free world" are over. Instead, American leadership now operates on a much older, darker principle: it only respects other societies based upon the extent to which it regards them as having a formidable military capacity.

Power respects power. Conversely, a nation that relies purely on its "moral standing" while neglecting its hard power is viewed by the current American political elite not as a noble ally, but as a vulnerable dependent ripe for exploitation. When Washington looks across its northern border, it must see an entity capable of inflicting unacceptable costs, not an economic territory to be absorbed at zero political or military expense.

II. Dismantling the Architecture of Dependency

To escape the gravitational pull of Washington’s sphere of influence, Canada must first dismantle the structural mechanisms that allow American leaders to claim they "protect" us. The fundamental prerequisite for true sovereignty is the outright rejection of NORAD and its unified command structure as it currently stands. For decades, NORAD has served as a rhetorical weapon for Washington, allowing successive U.S. presidents to depict Canada as a security parasite.

Walking away from this integrated binational command forces a hard, necessary recalibration. It permanently disables American leverage and shifts Canada from an American protectorate to a self-determined power capable of managing its own domain. As long as our aerospace and maritime defence are fundamentally tethered to Colorado Springs, Canada’s political independence remains compromised.

In place of NORAD, Canada must move away from defensive asymmetric models that assume we must simply hide in the bush while our centralized infrastructure is obliterated. Rumoured scenarios of passive territorial defence lack true deterrent focus; they are blueprints for a managed surrender, assuming Canada must absorb the blow while America remains structurally untouched.

Instead, Canada must adopt a doctrine of decentralized, quasi-symmetrical warfare—countervailing an enormous, unified military monolith with a very nimble, highly distributed structure capable of autonomous strategic decision-making even in the event of the destruction of a centralized command based in Ottawa.

This doctrine draws directly from the adaptive, small-unit tactics of Canadian military history, while leveraging the unique demographic reality of modern Canadian multiculturalism. A diverse, multilingual population provides an unparalleled pool of talent for global intelligence networks, information systems, and community-entrenched cells capable of operating independently across any theatre. By ensuring every regional unit has the authority and capability to make independent strategic decisions, Canada removes the vulnerabilities inherent to a massive, top-heavy military opponent. If there is no central command node to decapitate, the enemy is forced to fight a war against a thousand independent, self-directed cells.

III. The Six-Layer Web of Defence

To achieve true deterrence, Canada's territorial defence must consist of an intricate, six-layer web of defence totaling roughly one million personnel. This total-defence society would be structured across overlapping spheres of authority designed to make a swift or bloodless occupation a structural impossibility:

The Core Spine: The first layer consists of the professional Canadian Armed Forces and its primary reserves. This force serves as the high-tech, strategic backbone of the defence web, managing advanced anti-access/area-denial (A2/AD) missile systems, cyber warfare operations, and heavy strategic logistics, providing the necessary conventional anchoring for the broader decentralized forces.The Provincial Bastions: The second layer establishes newly established provincial militias operating directly under the authority of each respective provincial government. This ensures that regional defence cannot be decapitated by a strike on the federal capital. Tailored to their unique geography—whether the dense forests of Ontario, the vast prairies, or the rugged terrain of British Columbia—these units turn every province into an independent, heavily armed fortress.The Civic Shield: The third layer deploys the Canadian People’s Corps, managed at the municipal level by every city and town. These civic units are deeply embedded within local communities, responsible for securing local critical infrastructure, water supplies, localized communication grids, and urban sectors.The Grassroots Edge: The fourth layer forms community-based Crown Militias led by Canadian veterans, citizens with verified foreign military backgrounds, and energetic reserve personnel. These highly flexible units are built to motivate and mobilize specific diaspora and local communities into autonomous, self-sustaining patriot defence cells, turning Canada's diverse demographic landscape into an impenetrable network of grassroots resistance.The Indigenous Sovereign Shield: The critical fifth layer empowers all Indigenous nations to rejuvenate their traditional-knowledge military defence capabilities. By being fully armed and integrated into their own territorial defence systems, First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities can use their absolute, unmatched generational knowledge of the land to completely swallow and defeat an advancing military force—mirroring the decentralized tactical supremacy that defeated the United States in Vietnam. Crucially, this layer recognizes that military readiness requires profound social healing. True preparedness within this layer is fundamentally guaranteed by ensuring robust, unyielding support for the holistic health, healthcare infrastructure, and community well-being of Indigenous peoples.The Forward Deterrent: The sixth and final layer introduces a revolutionary forward deterrent: replacing our integrated American ties with formal European Union, Commonwealth, and Francophonie Defence Pacts. Rather than waiting to absorb an invasion, permanent international troops stationed across Canadian territory from these allied blocs would be legally bound to a forward-leaning posture. An American aggression would no longer be an isolated border skirmish; it would instantly trigger an international crisis involving global partners, creating an immediate international tripwire system on Canadian soil.

IV. The Legal Architecture of Total Defence: Navigating the Federal-Provincial Fracture

The primary structural vulnerability of any centralized state facing a near-peer or superior military threat is the illusion of a single point of failure. If an adversary can decapitate the federal executive in Ottawa, the national will to resist is theoretically broken. To prevent this, Canada's six-layer defence web utilizes a radical, legally decentralized framework that distributes command authority directly down to provincial Premiers, municipal councils, and Indigenous sovereign leadership, ensuring that the legal continuity of the state survives the physical destruction of the national capital.

Under the current statutory architecture of the Emergencies Act and the National Defence Act, military command flows strictly from the federal Cabinet down through the Chief of the Defence Staff. However, in an existential total-defence scenario, this top-heavy command line is deliberately augmented by provincial emergency legislation and recognized treaty sovereignty. By invoking provincial Emergency Management Acts simultaneously across all ten provinces, Premiers possess the statutory authority to mobilize and command localized civil defence forces independent of federal infrastructure.

The interaction between these layers is governed by three precise operational parameters:

Autonomous Regional Succession: Should communication with the federal Cabinet be severed or compromised by cyber warfare, provincial Premiers automatically assume supreme command over all military and paramilitary personnel within their borders. The newly formed provincial militias operate as distinct legal entities under provincial jurisdiction, legally insulated from federal surrender or centralized compromise.The Municipal Police Mandate: At the local level, the Canadian People’s Corps functions under the legal umbrella of municipal police services acts and local emergency bylaws. By tying municipal units to local law enforcement mandates, local councils retain the explicit legal right to arm and deploy citizens to protect local critical infrastructure, water networks, and communication grids, effectively preventing foreign forces from establishing administrative control over Canadian cities.Indigenous Operational Autonomy: Mirroring the inherent rights of self-government, the Indigenous Sovereign Shield operates under its own traditional and contemporary leadership councils. Free from the potential bureaucratic paralysis of Ottawa, these nations hold autonomous jurisdiction over their territorial spaces, turning the vast northern and rural topographies into thousands of untamable defensive sectors.

V. The Psychological Matrix: Shattering the Pentagon Calculus

For Washington’s military planners, the prospect of an intervention in Canada has traditionally been modelled as a rapid, high-intensity logistical exercise—a conventional campaign reliant on overwhelming air superiority, rapid armoured thrusts along major highway corridors, and the immediate seizure of key political nodes. The realization that they face an army of one million decentralized, deeply entrenched defenders distributed across a six-layer vertical defence web completely shatters this tactical paradigm, transforming a predictable occupation model into an unmanageable logistical and psychological nightmare.

Modern American military doctrine is optimized for network-centric warfare against a symmetrical state adversary with identifiable centres of gravity. When applied to Canada's defence web, the Pentagon's analytical models fail due to three distinct psychological disruptions:

The Invalidation of Kinetic Targeting: Conventional air superiority and long-range precision missile strikes lose their strategic utility when there are no centralized headquarters, supply depots, or uniform command structures to target. When facing a million decentralized combatants distributed among autonomous provincial militias, municipal corps, community-led Crown Militias, and Indigenous nations utilizing traditional-knowledge tactical dispersion, the enemy's targeting cycles become obsolete. Planners are forced to realize that every intersection, municipal water facility, and rural township is an independent, self-directed fortress that must be cleared manually.The Infinite Attrition Equation: Pentagon planners operate under strict timelines dictated by political expediency and economic sustainability. A conflict that cannot be resolved in days or weeks poses an immediate threat to domestic American stability. The math of occupying a nation of Canada's immense geographic scale against a million highly motivated, community-entrenched defenders forces planners to calculate an unacceptable casualty rate, draining the political will of the invading administration before a single boot touches the ground.The Information Mirror Crisis: The most acute psychological threat to the invading force is the realization that Canada's defence web is built to look back into the United States. Knowing that Canadian Crown Militias leverage a deeply multicultural, hyper-connected diaspora that can communicate directly with American civil society forces Pentagon planners to anticipate immediate domestic political blowback. Every military movement inside Canada is instantly transmitted, analysed, and framed to the American public not as a march to victory, but as an illegitimate, anti-democratic exercise in authoritarianism, inducing deep operational paralysis within the U.S. military chain of command itself.

VI. Grounding the Paradigm: The Historical Precedents of Total Defence

The concept of a total-defence society is neither a modern invention nor an untested theory; it is the historically proven method by which smaller, highly self-aware nations preserve their sovereignty when forced to live in the shadow of aggressive, expansive superpowers. By structuring its defence around an armed, decentralized populace, Canada directly adopts the successful strategic doctrines of societies like Switzerland, Sweden, and Finland.

These historical frameworks provide the necessary real-world validation for the Canadian six-layer web:

The Swiss Reduit and Universal Readiness: Throughout the 20th century, Switzerland maintained its independence surrounded by hostile totalitarian powers by implementing the Reduit strategy—a doctrine of making the cost of an invasion structurally ruinous. By ensuring that every citizen was trained, armed, and capable of destroying localized infrastructure to deny it to an invader, the Swiss proved that a highly organized, decentralized population can successfully deter a vastly superior military machine. Canada's integration of Crown Militias and provincial forces directly mirrors this architecture of total societal denial.The Finnish Model of Comprehensive Security: Finland’s entire national identity is built upon the institutional memory of resisting asymmetric aggression through total societal mobilization coordinated by the Finnish Ministry of Defence. The Finnish model binds together corporate supply chains, municipal services, and a massive citizen reserve into a single, seamless defence grid. Finland demonstrates that true deterrence is achieved when an adversary realizes that crossing the border means engaging not just an army, but an entire society functioning as a unified defensive system.The Swedish Total Defence Integration: Sweden's historical and modern Totalförsvaret (Total Defence) doctrine, overseen by the Swedish Civil Contingencies Agency (MSB), explicitly dictates that every element of society—from civil defence to psychological operations—must be organized to resist external aggression. The Swedish model places a heavy emphasis on psychological resilience, ensuring that any message of surrender from a centralized source is legally ignored by local cells. By adopting these proven Nordic and Alpine blueprints, Canada moves away from experimental theory and steps into a time-tested tradition of sovereign self-reliance, proving that a dedicated democracy can permanently hold its ground against the ambitions of any empire.

VII. Turning the Weapon of Legitimacy Against Fascism

Crucially, this six-layer web completely alters the strategic calculus of Washington’s political elites by making the cost of an attack on Canada so severe that it threatens the destruction and dissolution of America itself. True deterrence cannot mean fighting a war of attrition solely on Canadian soil; it means ensuring that the consequences of aggression bleed instantly and devastatingly into the American homeland.

To achieve this, Canadian foreign policy and information warfare must actively strike back at the un-American nature of a Washington regime that would violate its closest democratic neighbour. Supporters of the six-layer vertical defence system must aggressively emphasize that an attack on Canada is the ultimate manifestation of fascism—an action that fundamentally betrays the core values of liberty and freedom that everyday Americans cherish.

Canadian statecraft should openly co-opt and quote explicit warnings from high-ranking American institutional figures, such as former Vice President Kamala Harris, who famously warned voters that Donald Trump sought to emulate the authoritarian rise of mid-20th century dictators, or former White House Chief of Staff John Kelly, who stated unequivocally in reports documented by CBC News that his executive impulses mirrored Nazism. By systematically highlighting these internal American warnings, Canadian communications can spark an immediate cascade effect of disaffection, triggering a crisis of legitimacy within civil society, the media, and split factions of the U.S. military chain of command itself.

Mark Carney and other visionary leaders have already taken vital steps to alert both Canadians and international allies to the potentially imminent nature of this U.S. aggression. However, Canada’s leadership must now go far beyond the polite, traditional rhetoric of a middle power. It is no longer enough to merely assert Canadian sovereignty or lodge complaints at international forums.

Carney and our political class must step forward as the willing leaders of a Canadian economic, political, and military superpower—a nation fully united across six unbreakable layers of societal defence, prepared to defend its sovereignty to the absolute end. By standing tall as a formidable bastion of liberty, Canada will not only command the caution of Washington's planners, but will inspire freedom-loving Americans themselves to rise up, resist fascism, and topple any lawless administration that dares to cross our border.

news.title: Republican senator says his own party are ‘tone deaf’ as GOP spends millions to try to hold back Democratic blue wave
news.text:
National Republican campaign groups are pouring massive sums into Senate races across the country as fresh polling indicates the party is struggling to defend typically reliable red territory ahead of the midterms. 

The National Republican Senatorial Committee has launched a $46 million ad campaign across key states - allocating $11 million to Ohio, $9 million to Iowa, $8 million to North Carolina and $2 million to Alaska, according to the New York Post. 

Additionally, the Senate Leadership Fund — a political action committee aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune — is putting $100 million behind Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, with plans to keep buying airtime through Election Day. Recent surveys, such as a Marist College Poll, show Paxton trailing Democrat James Talarico, 44 percent to 50 percent. 

Senator Jim Justice, a West Virginia Republican, openly criticized his party’s current approach.

“You’ve got Republicans scrambling everywhere,” Justice told the publication. “When — my lord of living, all we had to do was really be in touch with the people four or five months ago … We’ve done all kinds of great stuff. You know, but we’re tone deaf in a lot of ways.”

A source familiar with the strategy told the Post that the heavy spending was a “red wall kind of thing,” and added: “We only spend money where we think we can make a difference.” 

The financial push highlights growing concerns inside the party about both congressional chambers. With Republicans holding a tight 53-47 Senate majority, a loss of just four seats would hand control back toDemocrats.

Republican candidates in traditionally conservative states are increasingly breaking with the White House on key issues as their polling numbers slip. 

In Ohio, where President Donald Trump won by 13 points over Kamala Harris in the 2024 White House race, former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown now holds a 4-point lead over appointed Republican Senator Jon Husted. Quantus Insights puts the race in a virtual deadlock, with Brown at 45.6 percent to Husted's 45.3 percent.

Husted recently said the Iran war “needs to come to an end as quickly as possible,” though he abstained from a War Powers resolution vote Thursday that aimed to stop military action.

In Iowa, which Trump won with 56 percent of the vote, Democrat Josh Turek is deadlocked with Republican Ashley Hinson. A recent Marist College Poll puts Turek at 50 percent to Hinson’s 42 percent among registered voters.

Political analysts are adjusting their forecasts accordingly. Larry Sabato shifted Iowa to a “toss-up” and Kansas to “leans Republican,” while the Cook Political Report moved 15 House seats toward Democrats Friday, including changing New Jersey Representative Tom Kean’s seat to “lean Democrat.”

Erin Covey, of the Cook Political Report, told the Post that Ohio and Iowa “look especially dire for Republicans” because of tariffs and rising gas prices.

“What’s worse environmentally for them compared to 2018 is the economy,” Covey said, citing the midterm election in which Democrats flipped 40 House seats. 

Cook Political Report analyst Amy Walter wrote that the economy had turned into an “anvil” for Trump, making it risky for him to campaign in competitive areas where his presence could drive up Democratic turnout. 

Tracking polls from Economist/YouGov show Trump underwater in every state except Idaho, Wyoming and West Virginia. His upcoming campaign swings are set for safe Republican territory in Oklahoma and Alabama rather than battlegrounds.

In Kansas, where a Republican hasn’t lost a Senate race in 100 years, Senator Roger Marshall is clinging to a narrow polling lead. The latest Emerson College Polling-Nextar Media Survey shows Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton at 45 percent to Marshall’s 43 percent.

“When ICE operates in Kansas, it needs to coordinate with our local law enforcement,” Marshall said Thursday following immigration sweeps in the state. 

Party strategists believe big ad spending and Democratic divisions over socialism will help them hold off the challenge. 

“A lot of our races are being nationalized,” the Republican source told the New York Post, but noted that “Iowa, New Hampshire, Maine – those places are still very siloed” with local factors that give GOP candidates an edge.
news.summary: ‘You’ve got Republicans scrambling everywhere’
news.author: Jasmine Fernández

news.title: Trump presidency ‘as we know it’ ends in Nov, Newsom says | Kuwait Times Newspaper
news.text:
NEW YORK: California Governor Gavin Newsom has a prediction for November: Democrats retake the House, and Donald Trump’s presidency “as we know it” is over. “We’re going to take back the House of Representatives. It’s a day of reckoning, a new day coming,” Newsom told AFP and two other outlets, after a UN climate summit in New York. “Trump’s presidency, as we know it, ends in November,” said the 58-year-old outgoing Democratic leader of the nation’s most populous state, widely seen as a leading contender for his party’s 2028 presidential nomination. Newsom, who spoke in an interview Wednesday as part of a journalism initiative called Covering Climate Now, did not give details on how he thinks a Democratic win would in essence end the Trump presidency.

But if Trump’s Republicans lose control of one or both houses of Congress, Democrats can in fact curb the president’s expansive agenda—though the executive still wields considerable power. Newsom also insisted climate was winning politics—if framed not as a “green” issue but as one tied to everything from grocery prices to home insurance to national security. “People say ‘why the hell are you talking about that, you should be talking about the kitchen table,’ I said ‘I am!’” He pointed to the price of beef and coffee, and the challenges of insuring a home or getting a mortgage amid growing climate risks from more extreme wildfires to coastal erosion supercharged by El Nino.

California a green pioneer

Other politicians shy away from the subject, he said, “because they don’t know how to talk about it, and those that have talked about in the past have been accused of being soft, weak, effete, green, hyperbolic.” He conceded that “some of our language did get a little apocalyptic.” The key, he said, is hammering home that “it’s not about electric power; it’s about economic power. It’s about statecraft.”

At the summit, he pitched California as proof that climate action and growth go hand in hand, saying the state—the world’s fourth-largest economy, whose GDP has grown 40 percent since 2019 - had run on 100 percent clean energy for at least part of the day on 90 percent of days this year. His administration has battled Trump and congressional Republicans over efforts to undo California’s green rules—from scrapping its planned phase-out of gasoline cars to paying companies to abandon offshore wind projects.

“Donald Trump wants to recreate the 19th century,” said Newsom. “He’s doubling down on stupid. He’s putting America in reverse.” “Whoever the nominee is of the Democratic Party is going to be the next president of the United States,” he said. Any of the Democratic hopefuls, he added, would be “exponentially better than a Rubio or Vance that have countenanced this corruption, this grift, this graft, this destruction of truth and trust and institutions,” referring to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance. They are seen as the likely Republican front-runners, though neither has declared.

‘Old rules don’t apply’ 

Left-wing Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez made waves this week when she told The New York Times she was weighing a run, musing about whether a Latina could win in a country that rejected female nominees in 2016 and 2024. AOC, Newsom and Jon Ossoff, a charismatic Jewish senator from Georgia, are among the favorites on betting markets. “She absolutely could become the nominee of the party. That’s my assessment of electability. This notion that a woman can’t win is insulting,” Newsom said, blaming “punditry” for perpetuating the trope. “I’m done with people talking like that. Or that if you’re from California or you’re Jewish or you’re old or you’re too young—give me a damn break. Our politics is completely scrambled post-Trump. The old rules, they do not apply.”

Though he called Ocasio-Cortez a “generational talent,” he pointedly did not rule out running against her—having told CNN emphatically last week that he would not challenge Kamala Harris, the 2024 nominee, with whom he shares a history in California that predates politics. “It’s a different framework,” he said. “I don’t have a relationship that goes back to before we were both in politics. I don’t have a relationship in the context of our base overlaying in remarkable ways. Whether Newsom runs, he said, depends on whether he can “look them and you in the eye and say I have something unique they don’t... voice, experience, perspective, capacity that is unique and distinctive.” - AFP
news.author: Kuwait Times

news.title: Ocasio-Cortez downplays 2028 speculation, stresses 2026 elections
news.text: Days after raising speculation about her 2028 prospects in a New York Times interview, U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said she is focused on helping Democrats — including herself — win reelection in 2026.Ocasio-Cortez has recently been the subject of speculation about a possible 2028 Democratic presidential bid, a race expected to draw a crowded field. Some prediction markets list her among the leading Democratic contenders.Potential candidates include Democratic governors Gavin Newsom of California, Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania and Andy Beshear of Kentucky. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, Sens. Jon Ossoff of Georgia and Mark Kelly of Arizona, and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg also are viewed as possible contenders.RELATED STORY | Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is reportedly weighing a possible presidential run“Our next election is in November,” Ocasio-Cortez told reporters. “2028 is two years away. My focus is on this year.”Earlier this week, Ocasio-Cortez traveled to upstate New York, far from her New York City-based district, to campaign for Democrats hoping to regain control of the House in November’s election.During a campaign speech, she said she understands why some voters have not been motivated to support Democratic candidates.RELATED STORY | Brief 9/11 ceremony exchange between Mamdani, AOC sparks political backlash“This has been such a hurtful and divisive and horrible time where we have seen some of the worst of human nature emerge — corruption, racism, bigotry, just all of it laid bare,” she said. “It’s not surprising to me that oftentimes turnout is not the same as it was in 2020 because what a lot of people are seeing is, in the wake of all of this depravity, they do not see leaders standing up courageously to defend against it.”
news.summary: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said her focus is on helping Democrats win in 2026, downplaying speculation about a 2028 presidential bid.

news.title: I’m A Woman Who Did A Solo Walk Across Europe. Here’s The 1 Thing Most Men — Even The ‘Good Guys’ — Don’t Understand.
news.text:
My physical therapist and I were chatting about his recent trip to the Alaskan wilderness while he watched me do another slow squat. I almost sank to the ground when he said, “It’s necessary, now and then, to be in the presence of grizzly bears. To be reminded that we are not the apex predators.” 

Women do not need to go to Alaska to be taught this lesson (nor does anyone who isn’t an able-bodied, heterosexual white man). Women constantly face real danger while we are just trying to navigate our lives, out in the world and, for some, sadly, at home. 

My physical therapist was unironically proud of his humility. Humility is a start, but it isn’t what women need from men. We need empathy. Psychologist Marshall Rosenberg, who developed nonviolent communication, said, “Our ability to offer empathy can allow us to stay vulnerable, defuse potential violence.”

The physical therapist is helping me recover from a knee surgery and prepare me for my hike next summer, 3,000 miles along the Continental Divide Trail. But he is not the only apex predator to set my teeth on edge. Because of my online searches for a lightweight tent and a water filter more effective than the heavy dinosaur I’ve been hauling around for years, the all-knowing algorithm has blessed my feed with clips and reels of rosy-cheeked long-distance hikers, newly off-trail and still flush with exhilaration. In one interview, I watched a young man who is asked, “Why? Why do it?” As if they have all memorized the same script, he answers, “When was the last time you were in danger? Real physical danger?” 

Could he be any more oblivious? I believe the enthusiastic young man in the interview, like my physical therapist, is well-intentioned. He has gone through an empowering experience and wants to encourage others to do the same. But his journey only reconfirmed what he has already been taught by our culture. He emerges all-powerful or, in other words, unchanged. 

Women need men — the real apex predators — to understand the danger they pose to us. At the moment, our country is backsliding. Women are being stripped of our right to bodily autonomy in a way that men would never tolerate and, historically, have never had to. In his confirmation hearing for a seat on the Supreme Court, Brett Kavanaugh famously drew a blank when Kamala Harris asked him to think of a law — any law — that affected only men’s bodies. We just elected an adjudicated abuser for president. The clear signal to men: Women are prey. We are still prey. Many men, and even young boys, have heard that message and are now gleefully chanting, “Your body, my choice.”

In our patriarchal culture, where power is concentrated among men, their survival does not depend on empathy. Ours does. The point, however, is not to make men feel as unsafe as women do — that will only encourage them to scramble for more power. The goal is for men to want women to be as safe as men are, to understand that we are not, and to act toward a real remedy: changing the assumptions and behaviors of men.

What if, during the interview, the hiker had wondered: When was the last time someone else experienced real physical danger? Imagine him asking someone and listening to their response. Or just using his own imagination to supply answers. How do we encourage men to notice — and care — about a truth they mostly don’t experience? We must teach them, one conversation at a time. This is an unfair burden, but I believe it is the only way. It’s tempting to tell men to figure it out on their own, and I would never judge anyone for saying, “Nope, I choose not to do this work.” Whether women engage in teaching conversations is — always — our choice. 

Since I wrote a viral article about fear and walking a thousand miles alone across Europe, I’ve had several interesting interviews and podcast conversations with men — a hopeful sign. One time, the interviewer, Paul, asked why I walk long distances. I answered that it gave me a chance to fall back in love with the world, the details of which, when I take time to notice, are stunningly beautiful. “And hilarious,” I said. “People especially.”

“Hilarious? What do you mean?” he asked. I paused for a moment to take in the fact that he had actually asked me a follow-up question. But soon he circled around to the question everyone asks: Was I afraid of walking alone? They mean: afraid of men. But before I could answer this time, Paul jumped in with a story of his own: 

“Every night at home, I take my dog out for a walk, and every night one of my neighbors takes her dog for a walk. Whenever I pass by, I can tell she tightens up. I don’t understand,” he said, exasperated. “She’s met me before, once even with my wife. I’m starting to feel a little insulted.”

I heard the unspoken challenge: Weren’t we women taking this a little too far? Hadn’t he proved to his neighbor that he meant no harm? Come on — he was one of the good guys. I considered sighing in disappointment or bristling in outrage — but before his interruption, he had asked thoughtful questions and even wanted me to elaborate on my answers. He was paying attention. That was an open door, and I chose to walk through it.

“Most of the assaults I have experienced,” I said, “were carried out by men I had known for years, who I had been alone with numerous times: my uncle, my college professor, my doctor. 

“They didn’t assault me,” I said, “until they did.” 

“Ohhh,” he said, the hackles in his voice softening. “What can I do,” he asked me then, “to make things better?” 

Because he seemed genuinely open, I decided to go one step further. “Talk to men,” I said. “You teach them.” 

When I go on a long hike, I aim to be soft, to allow the soul-clearing scent of pine sap baking in the heat, the sound of wind gathering itself on its way up a hillside, the electrical hum that precedes a crack of lightning on a ridge or the dangerously heavy pull of water on a river crossing to remind me how alive I am and how much my own racing heart is part of the rhythm of the world. I am alert but unafraid.

Men, don’t miss the real opportunity that such a long hike offers: a chance to look beyond your own experience and pay attention to the impact of your words and actions. You can exhibit real bravery by going where few men have tread before you. Ask questions. Listen to our answers, and show us some empathy.

Right now, the stakes for women could not be higher. If you consider yourself a “good guy,” the alarm bells should be ringing in your head, too. It is time for you to stand up and pay more attention. Not assaulting women is not enough. It is time for you to take up the burden of educating your brothers, other “good guys” who think they get it but don’t. The hill we women have been climbing toward full citizenship just got a lot steeper and more treacherous. We invite men to join us, but they are going to have to start carrying their own weight.

Lea Page’s work has appeared in New York Times, Washington Post and The Guardian. She is the author of “Parenting in the Here and Now” (Floris Books, 2015) and is at work on another book about paying attention.

My physical therapist and I were chatting about his recent trip to the Alaskan wilderness while he watched me do another slow squat. I almost sank to the ground when he said, “It’s necessary, now and then, to be in the presence of grizzly bears. To be reminded that we are not the apex predators.” 

Women do not need to go to Alaska to be taught this lesson (nor does anyone who isn’t an able-bodied, heterosexual white man). Women constantly face real danger while we are just trying to navigate our lives, out in the world and, for some, sadly, at home. 

My physical therapist was unironically proud of his humility. Humility is a start, but it isn’t what women need from men. We need empathy. Psychologist Marshall Rosenberg, who developed nonviolent communication, said, “Our ability to offer empathy can allow us to stay vulnerable, defuse potential violence.”

The physical therapist is helping me recover from a knee surgery and prepare me for my hike next summer, 3,000 miles along the Continental Divide Trail. But he is not the only apex predator to set my teeth on edge. Because of my online searches for a lightweight tent and a water filter more effective than the heavy dinosaur I’ve been hauling around for years, the all-knowing algorithm has blessed my feed with clips and reels of rosy-cheeked long-distance hikers, newly off-trail and still flush with exhilaration. In one interview, I watched a young man who is asked, “Why? Why do it?” As if they have all memorized the same script, he answers, “When was the last time you were in danger? Real physical danger?” 

Could he be any more oblivious? I believe the enthusiastic young man in the interview, like my physical therapist, is well-intentioned. He has gone through an empowering experience and wants to encourage others to do the same. But his journey only reconfirmed what he has already been taught by our culture. He emerges all-powerful or, in other words, unchanged. 

Women need men — the real apex predators — to understand the danger they pose to us. At the moment, our country is backsliding. Women are being stripped of our right to bodily autonomy in a way that men would never tolerate and, historically, have never had to. In his confirmation hearing for a seat on the Supreme Court, Brett Kavanaugh famously drew a blank when Kamala Harris asked him to think of a law — any law — that affected only men’s bodies. We just elected an adjudicated abuser for president. The clear signal to men: Women are prey. We are still prey. Many men, and even young boys, have heard that message and are now gleefully chanting, “Your body, my choice.”

In our patriarchal culture, where power is concentrated among men, their survival does not depend on empathy. Ours does. The point, however, is not to make men feel as unsafe as women do — that will only encourage them to scramble for more power. The goal is for men to want women to be as safe as men are, to understand that we are not, and to act toward a real remedy: changing the assumptions and behaviors of men.

What if, during the interview, the hiker had wondered: When was the last time someone else experienced real physical danger? Imagine him asking someone and listening to their response. Or just using his own imagination to supply answers. How do we encourage men to notice — and care — about a truth they mostly don’t experience? We must teach them, one conversation at a time. This is an unfair burden, but I believe it is the only way. It’s tempting to tell men to figure it out on their own, and I would never judge anyone for saying, “Nope, I choose not to do this work.” Whether women engage in teaching conversations is — always — our choice. 

Since I wrote a viral article about fear and walking a thousand miles alone across Europe, I’ve had several interesting interviews and podcast conversations with men — a hopeful sign. One time, the interviewer, Paul, asked why I walk long distances. I answered that it gave me a chance to fall back in love with the world, the details of which, when I take time to notice, are stunningly beautiful. “And hilarious,” I said. “People especially.”

“Hilarious? What do you mean?” he asked. I paused for a moment to take in the fact that he had actually asked me a follow-up question. But soon he circled around to the question everyone asks: Was I afraid of walking alone? They mean: afraid of men. But before I could answer this time, Paul jumped in with a story of his own: 

“Every night at home, I take my dog out for a walk, and every night one of my neighbors takes her dog for a walk. Whenever I pass by, I can tell she tightens up. I don’t understand,” he said, exasperated. “She’s met me before, once even with my wife. I’m starting to feel a little insulted.”

I heard the unspoken challenge: Weren’t we women taking this a little too far? Hadn’t he proved to his neighbor that he meant no harm? Come on — he was one of the good guys. I considered sighing in disappointment or bristling in outrage — but before his interruption, he had asked thoughtful questions and even wanted me to elaborate on my answers. He was paying attention. That was an open door, and I chose to walk through it.

“Most of the assaults I have experienced,” I said, “were carried out by men I had known for years, who I had been alone with numerous times: my uncle, my college professor, my doctor. 

“They didn’t assault me,” I said, “until they did.” 

“Ohhh,” he said, the hackles in his voice softening. “What can I do,” he asked me then, “to make things better?” 

Because he seemed genuinely open, I decided to go one step further. “Talk to men,” I said. “You teach them.” 

When I go on a long hike, I aim to be soft, to allow the soul-clearing scent of pine sap baking in the heat, the sound of wind gathering itself on its way up a hillside, the electrical hum that precedes a crack of lightning on a ridge or the dangerously heavy pull of water on a river crossing to remind me how alive I am and how much my own racing heart is part of the rhythm of the world. I am alert but unafraid.

Men, don’t miss the real opportunity that such a long hike offers: a chance to look beyond your own experience and pay attention to the impact of your words and actions. You can exhibit real bravery by going where few men have tread before you. Ask questions. Listen to our answers, and show us some empathy.

Right now, the stakes for women could not be higher. If you consider yourself a “good guy,” the alarm bells should be ringing in your head, too. It is time for you to stand up and pay more attention. Not assaulting women is not enough. It is time for you to take up the burden of educating your brothers, other “good guys” who think they get it but don’t. The hill we women have been climbing toward full citizenship just got a lot steeper and more treacherous. We invite men to join us, but they are going to have to start carrying their own weight.

Lea Page’s work has appeared in New York Times, Washington Post and The Guardian. She is the author of “Parenting in the Here and Now” (Floris Books, 2015) and is at work on another book about paying attention.

news.title: US midterm elections just weeks away, but these two frontrunners could be leading their parties in 2028 presidential primaries
news.text:
US midterm elections 2026: Kamala Harris and JD Vance emerge as early 2028 presidential front-runners in new poll

2026 US midterm elections: The 2026 midterm elections are still weeks away, yet the first signs of the 2028 presidential race are already appearing. A new poll has former Vice President Kamala Harris leading the Democratic field and Vice President JD Vance ahead among Republicans. Neither has announced a campaign, so the numbers are better read as an early measure of name recognition and interest than a picture of a settled primary.The McLaughlin & Associates poll was conducted from Sept. 16 through Sept. 22 among 463 likely voters. Fifteen percent said they were undecided. Among Republicans, Vance had 35%, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio at 15% and Donald Trump Jr. at 14%. Twelve percent remained undecided.Harris has a lead, but the Democratic field is still wide openHarris' 29% puts her well ahead of Newsom in this particular survey. That does not mean Democrats have decided on their 2028 nominee. There is no formal primary field yet, and several of the names being discussed have not said they will run.Newsom's own comments show how much could still change. Earlier this month, he told CNN's Jake Tapper that he would not run for president in 2028 if Harris decided to seek the nomination. He made the comment during a conversation in Montana about his political plans. It was not an announcement of a campaign, but it gave a clear indication of how Harris' decision could affect another major Democratic contender.Vance is ahead while Rubio keeps his distance from 2028 talkThe Republican numbers are more striking at the top. Vance's 35% is more than twice Rubio's 15% in the McLaughlin survey. Trump Jr. is close behind Rubio at 14%, while 12% of Republican respondents have not chosen anyone.Live EventsVance's position comes before any formal 2028 campaign.For now, the poll only shows where Republican preferences stand in an early hypothetical contest.Rubio has also tried to cool down speculation about his own plans. During an official visit to Colombia earlier this month, he said he had no plans to run for anything at the moment and said he was focused on his current responsibilities.Ted Cruz is open about wanting the presidencyTexas Sen. Ted Cruz has been less reserved when asked about his long-term ambitions. In August, he told Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick that it was no secret he wanted to be president. When asked whether he would make another presidential run, Cruz left the timing open.That puts Cruz in a different position from Rubio, but it still falls short of a campaign announcement. The same basic uncertainty surrounds the leading names in the latest poll. Harris and Vance may be leading early hypothetical fields, but neither has officially entered the 2028 contest.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Politico Appears To Be Addicted to 'Crack'
news.text:
Here a Crack. There a Crack. Everywhere a Crack Crack!

Yes, if Politico is seeing cracks (of the GOP variety) then you know it must be election season. And right on cue with a little over a month left until the midterm elections Politico is seeing huge cracks in the Republican party. In fact they are so insistent on GOP cracks that you almost get the sense they want Republican-inclined voters to get demoralized and neglect to vote this year.

For an example of how much Politico is desperately hyping the GOP Crack theme you need only to look at their Friday front page. The big crack headline at the top of that page (as of this writing) has a couple of Florida crackers, Gary Fineout and Kimberly Leonard, boldly declaring that things are so bad for the cracking GOP in Florida that they seem to need a life boat to rescue them from the inevitable: "‘We are hemorrhaging’: Cracks emerge in GOP’s Florida firewall."

Just a couple of stories down, Politico's Myah Ward and Erin Doherty gaze upon yet more emerging crack in "Poll: A crack is emerging in Trump’s coalition over deportations."

Let us now watch the "Cracks emerge in GOP's Florida Firewall," or at least what the pair of Florida crackers desperately want us to believe is emerging:

Now, some polling has shown statewide races inside the margin of error, including for governor and U.S. Senate. Democratic congressional seats seen as flippable after mid-decade redistricting are a question mark while some Republicans have distanced themselves from an increasingly unpopular president.Democratic wins in Florida would send tremors through the political ecosystem. It could not only help increase Democrats’ margins if they win back the House, but would also have a dramatic impact on the 2028 presidential race if Democrats win the governor’s race, given Florida has 30 electoral college votes up for grabs. Both Gov. Ron DeSantis and Trump won landslide victories in 2022 and 2024.

So "some polling has shown statewide races inside the margin of error?" Why, this could be the biggest crack in the Florida GOP since the 2018 gubernatorial election in that state when a Hopium infused Politico declared that "most polls show Gillum with a lead that’s within the margin of error or just outside it."

And now we analyze the other crack that Politico discovered emerging in "Trump’s coalition over deportations."

Non-MAGA Trump voters are more than twice as likely as self-identified MAGA Trump voters to say his mass deportation campaign is too aggressive, 31% to 14%. While roughly similar shares of both groups believe Trump’s campaign is about right, the MAGA base wants him to go even further: 36% of MAGA Trump voters say his campaign is not aggressive enough, compared with 23% of non-MAGA Trump voters.

Of course, we all know just how scientific political (push) polls are. Just ask Presidents Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris. The latter most likely would crack up with laughter over Politico's intoxication with the Friday overdose of Crack Hopium.
