news.title: The 30 greatest “Saturday Night Live” cast members, ranked
news.text:
Saturday Night Live is an institution, a proving ground for some of the best comedic talents in America to show what they’re made of in a fast-paced, chaotic environment without much of a safety net. After all, much of it unfolds live, and anything can go wrong. That’s what makes it all the more impressive when stars emerge with a variety of memorable characters, celebrity impressions, and well-delivered catchphrases that stick in the cultural consciousness for decades. SNL has seen plenty of performers leave without much fanfare, so the ones who stick it out tend to have the kind of longevity needed to make it in the entertainment industry.

With the late-night sketch series’ 52nd season now underway, we’re looking back on its most valuable players through the years. For this list, we’ve excluded alums who spent multiple seasons as anchors on Weekend Update (Tina Fey, Norm Macdonald, Seth Meyers, Amy Poehler, etc.). We’re also leaving out famous faces who found significantly greater success later on in their careers, so apologies to Joan Cusack, Michaela Watkins, Jenny Slate, Casey Wilson, Damon Wayans, Sarah Silverman, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Tim Robinson, and others. You know who you are. Don’t worry, we still love you!

So, without further ado, here’s our (highly subjective!) ranking of the 30 best Saturday Night Live players of all time.

Bobby Moynihan (9 seasons; 2008–2017)

While fellow repertory players Bill Hader, Kristen Wiig, and Kate McKinnon received much of the glory in the late-2000s to 2010s era, Bobby Moynihan was one of the clutch cast members we could rely on for a hearty laugh every week. Some of his best work came from behind the Weekend Update desk, particularly as the always-opinionated Drunk Uncle, secondhand news guy Anthony Crispino, or the obscenely orange Snooki from Jersey Shore.

Like many of the SNL greats, Moynihan’s comedic timing was sharp as a tack, but it was the way he modulated his voice depending on the character that helped him stand out. His mischievous grin was contagious, as was his chuckle that made it seem like he genuinely loved being on the show. And, of course, who could forget Ass Dan (RIP). —Kevin Jacobsen

Cheri Oteri (5 seasons; 1995–2000)

It’s wild to remember that Cheri Oteri’s first-ever onscreen work was SNL, considering how shot out of a cannon she was. Oteri’s zany, over-the-top characters and utter commitment to goofiness was a feat to behold. With a Jim Carrey-like elastic face and a voice that could project to the cheap seats, she quickly became one of the most valuable players of the late-‘90s.

Oteri’s performance as an impatient employee, Nadeen, is especially a comedic tour de force every time, nailing every line reading “Simmah down now!” But her gift for celebrity impressions also made her a key figure, most notably her recurring bit as Barbara Walters and her idiosyncratic high, breathy tone. It’s a shame that Oteri never got the kind of thriving film/TV career we expected following her 2000 departure compared to contemporaries like Will Ferrell or Molly Shannon, though it’s always a delight when she shows up in anything all these years later. —K.J.

Tracy Morgan (7 seasons; 1996–2003)

While Tracy Morganstruggled to find his voice on SNL at first, he certainly utilized it well in the seasons to come. Morgan made meals out of unusual characters such as exuberant Safari Planet host Brian Fellow or Astronaut Jones, a spaceman hopelessly distracted by the alien women he encounters. His genius was in making sketches work that would’ve been mind-numbingly flat in another actor’s hands through sheer, earnest commitment to the bit.

Of course, Morgan would find even greater success as Tracy Jordan on 30 Rock three years after leaving the sketch show. Series creator Tina Fey wrote the character with Morgan in mind, having worked with him extensively on SNL, and it was a true match made in heaven. His Emmy-nominated performance was the perfect project for Morgan, leaning into the unpredictable energy and childlike bluntness he excelled at on SNL. —K.J.

Mike Myers (7 seasons; 1989–1995)

Gifted chameleon Mike Myers was a master at creating instantly memorable SNL characters. The standout example is Wayne Campbell, who was such a hit he made two movies reprising his role as the metalhead during his tenure on the show. (Not to mention his later success with diverse comedic film roles, including Austin Powers, Dr. Evil, Fat Bastard, Shrek, and the Cat in the Hat...) 

“What Jerry Seinfeld said about me is that I’ve managed to break the rules of all American parody: I parody things that Americans don’t even know,” Myers told EW in 2008. “It’s been said of me that I can do comedy where comedy hadn’t previously existed.”

While this quote may sound boastful to some, he’s not wrong. In addition to Wayne Campbell, Myers’ time on SNL was filled with such great recurring bits, particularly as talk show hosts like Linda Richman of Coffee Talk (a.k.a. “Coffee Tawk”) or turtleneck-wearing, aggressively German Dieter of Sprockets. A true perfectionist, you could always count on Myers to deliver carefully constructed characters with internal lives and razor-sharp punchlines. —K.J.

Rachel Dratch (7 seasons; 1999–2006)

Toward the end of her fifth season, Rachel Dratch firmly cemented her name in SNL history thanks to debuting Debbie Downer. Her hilariously flat delivery in bringing up bad news — and bringing down the mood — made for comedy gold. But it wasn’t just the audience cracking up — that first Debbie Downer sketch shows the whole cast breaking character, with Jimmy Fallon and Horatio Sanz devolving into tearful laughter.

While Debbie Downer is her highlight, it’s only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to Dratch’s talent. One of the most underrated cast members during the show’s early-2000s seasons, Dratch rarely played the archetypical “straight woman” role reacting to the nonsense around her. She was the nonsense, playing brilliantly off her scene partners like Fallon as a pair of rowdy Boston teens or with Will Ferrell as the “Love-ahs.” —K.J.

Chris Parnell (8 seasons; 1998–2006)

Can you really be called one of the best cast members of all time if you were fired twice during your tenure on Saturday Night Live? If you’re bulletproof Everyman Chris Parnell you can. Possessed of a sonorous performer’s cadence that could switch registers from smarmy to silky as the sketch demanded, Parnell was the definition of the all-star utility player during his time on the show. Able to essay deadpan commercial pitchmen like Phil Hartman, plumb the depths of deliberately irritating weirdos like Will Forte, and anchor any number of quiz, talk, and news shows, Parnell had a sly, gleaming look in his eyes that suggested a lot more strangeness than his placid outer shell promised.

Like all undervalued utility players, Parnell found himself getting laid off by Lorne Michaels due to budget cuts not once, but twice, in 2001 and 2006. Parnell’s pitch-perfect performing composure is in full evidence in the 2013 sketch, “Centaur Job Interview,” where the eminently sensible centaur (Parnell, in half-horse prosthetic) patiently answers every invasively elaborate question Christopher Walken‘s interview can come up with. Still, the stalwart Parnell shone in his roles, no matter the size, and his invaluable comic presence served him well afterward, with Tina Fey remembering her SNL colleague for the scene-stealing role of Dr. Leo Spaceman on her series 30 Rock. Every team needs the perfect situational player off the bench, and Parnell was it, without question. —Dennis Perkins

Jason Sudeikis (9 seasons; 2005–2013)

There have been a fair number of Satans in Saturday Night Live history, but none so captured the essence as a performer than Jason Sudeikis‘ affably sinister prince of darkness. With his unassuming Midwestern handsomeness, Sudeikis threatens to get lost in the shuffle of blandly handsome SNL white guys — until he doesn’t. Recurring character Satan breezily explains all the delightful torments he’s proudest of (“Hey, d’you get that rash I sent you?,” he asks anchor Seth Meyers happily at one point), while ultimately taking offense at something deviously evil we humans have done, his Devil’s “what you see is what you get” assholery coming off, in Sudeikis’ hands, as irresistibly preferable in comparison.

While gamely playing the many comedy Everyman roles his general appearance and demeanor suggest him for, Sudeikis loved leaning into the strange as much as costars Will Forte, Fred Armisen, and Andy Samberg traditionally did, his grinning cheekiness putting his own unique spin on the proceedings. As an impressionist, Sudeikis remains the best Joe Biden, his white-toothed bluffness and occasional rambling a soul-match for the career politician and future president, while his riffing with Kristen Wiig as the gum-chewing “Two A-Holes“ mined Sudeikis’ sinister charm for huge, consistent laughs. In stacked and varied casts during his time on the show, Sudeikis more than held his own, displaying a star wattage (even while playing a dancing sidekick) that’s gone on to serve him especially well since leaving in 2013. —D.P.

Aidy Bryant (10 seasons; 2012–2022)

Bold, bubbly, and brilliantly adaptable, Aidy Bryant joined Cecily Strong and Kate McKinnon to form an unbeatable SNL trio during their time together. Blessed with a fearsome theatricality and a sweetly silly demeanor, Bryant slipped assuredly into every role with an infectious energy and a mischievous glint. While an expert at playing insecure teens and tweens with a delicate comic sensitivity, Bryant clearly relished knocking broader characters into the cheap seats, whether playing Tinker Bell’s crude bruiser of a sister or belting out the self-penned waterbed store jingle her proprietor husband had to constantly explain away.

One of Bryant’s most hilarious and affecting outings was as herself, writing a romantic sketch for two with dashing host Oscar Isaac: Bryant’s self-deprecating nature emerged in Isaac’s awkward but passionate wooing as he praised how much spaghetti she could eat and how she was “the most under-25 woman he’s ever met.” She and McKinnon were a can’t-miss team, their recurring doubles act as an ever-changing pair of glassy-eyed pitch-people for outlandish and ill-considered products and venues highlighting Bryant’s brilliance at matching her costars’ energy. —D.P.

Fred Armisen (11 seasons; 2002–2013)

Like costar Maya Rudolph, Fred Armisen is a comedy multi-instrument, his real-life musical talents combining with a limitless desire to channel his inner weirdness. A Fred Armisen sketch was often an exercise in escalating irritation, a comedy of manners where his character’s out-there nature disrupted audience comfort and expectation. Chameleonic in appearance and manner, Armisen could play it straight as well, but is best known for characterizations that skirt insufferableness, often to the point where the premise circles around again to begrudging hilarity.

Often centered on various unprofitable segments of the entertainment industry, Armisen’s best-known characters deconstruct the whole idea of performance as adopted personality, with that distinction bleeding into viewer perception of the drolly deadpan Armisen himself. Characters like Garth, the improvisational singer alongside Kristen Wiig’s Kat, pushed the duo’s self-impressed, deliberately off-putting schtick to viewer limits, and beyond. In one of the most divisive recurring sketches in SNL history, Armisen’s Stuart in “The Californians” joined his castmates in parodying soap opera mugging (and inexplicable obsession with driving directions) to a similar tolerance test. —D.P.

Cecily Strong (11 seasons; 2012–2022)

Viewers were spoiled for a decade by the presence of inseparable comedy partners Cecily Strong, Aidy Bryant, and Kate McKinnon. Strong had all the tools: a remarkable and versatile singing voice, impeccable acting chops, and a love of the belly laugh spotlight unrivaled even by her illustrious pals. Toss in an uncanny ability to channel some singularly unique celebrity voices and mannerisms (Maine Senator Susan Collins, Fox News host Jeanine Pirro, Senate independent Kyrsten Sinema), and Strong remains one of the most multi-talented women in the show’s history — and also its longest-running female cast member.

Strong also had a talent for the all-important Weekend Update featured commentator, traditionally an exercise in seizing upon one trait and mining it for every laugh available. Nobody did it better than Strong when portraying the self-important, barely listening cliché that is the Girl You Wish You Hadn’t Started a Conversation With at a Party, or Heather, the One-Dimensional Female Character from a Male-Driven Comedy, the actor turning types inside out and finding nothing but insightful laughs. Her turn as Goober the Clown, telling Strong’s own story about her abortion while wearing a red nose and honking a bicycle horn, is an all-time Update classic, a melding of vital political discourse with bracing silliness that will be shown forever. —D.P.

Molly Shannon (7 seasons; 1995–2001)

SNL has long been a welcoming home for misfit characters, and Molly Shannon nearly perfected the art of the overeager oddball. Case in point: Mary Katherine Gallagher, the mercurial Catholic schoolgirl who declares herself a “superstar” and has a rather unfortunate habit of sniffing her armpits when nervous. Shannon’s seemingly endless reserve of energy was best utilized in sketches heavy on physical comedy, such as her recurring Sally “I’m FIFTY!” O’Malley, a 50-year-old dancer who loves to demonstrate her ability to kick and stretch.

While SNL had largely been a boys’ club into the ‘90s, Shannon’s presence was an exuberant, desperately needed breath of fresh air. Her versatility as a performer laid the groundwork for future legends like Amy Poehler, Kristen Wiig, and Kate McKinnon to embrace their own eccentric weirdos. —K.J.

Jan Hooks (5 seasons; 1986–1991)

Now that both participants have passed on, watching the season 14 Schiller’s Reel short film “Love Is a Dream“ is a melancholic but heartwarming watch, with Jan Hooks and Phil Hartman doing a lovely choreographed dance to Bing Crosby’s “The Emperor Waltz.” Often teamed during their overlapping time on SNL, Hooks and Hartman were, indeed, a magnificent match, their offbeat and actorly styles bringing a grounded yet up-for-anything energy. Hooks could go for broke with the best of them, her Sweeney Sisters musical outings alongside Nora Dunn a throwback to Bill Murray‘s Nick the Lounge Singer in the duo’s channeling of over-the-top low-rent showbiz glitz.

But in sketches like 1990’s “Brenda the Waitress,” alongside Alec Baldwin, Hartman, Dunn, and Kevin Nealon, Hooks, as the hard-bitten waitress combatively bantering with Baldwin’s smooth-talking drifter, turned a five-minute SNL sketch into a showcase worthy of Off-Broadway comedy gold. Even when designated as the show’s go-to political wives (playing Betty Ford, Nancy Reagan, Elizabeth Dole, Kitty Dukakis, and Hillary Clinton as the years and elections marched on), Hooks’ consummate dedication to her characterizations made what could have been rote topical sketches into deft and arresting character pieces. —D.P.

Will Forte (8 seasons; 2002–2010)

It’s not that Will Forte wasn’t a valuable and integral part of the ensemble during his eight seasons on the show. It’s more that certain writer-performers are so singular in their comic style and vision that they carve out an easily identifiable yet impossible-to-encapsulate niche that brings a whole other element to the SNL mix. Such is the case with this former Groundling, whose bottomless energy and singular talent for strange and original comedy made it easy to pluck out his material from each week’s lineup. Originally tapped for the unenviable task of taking over as George W. Bush from the departed Will Ferrell, featured player Forte struggled until he became essentially the king of the “10-to-1” sketch, the last piece of the night, where his more outrageous and bizarre ideas could come out to play.

Legendarily teaming with Jason Sudeikis for the equal-parts baffling and uproarious “Potato Chip“ sketch, where the two equally committed actors build up a jaw-dropping head of steam as two men arguing over whether or not one has stolen a single piece of snack food, Forte’s peculiar imagination also brought us “the Falconer,” where his outdoorsman’s peril is constantly sidetracked by increasingly oddball adventures of his puppet falcon, Donald; and his recurring character MacGruber, a knockabout parody of TV’s MacGyver, whose personal insecurities invariably doom everyone in sight. No one could hold the camera’s gaze as wildly and fearlessly as Forte, the outsized yet contained madness of his characters courting audience confusion as much as laughter. —D.P.

Darrell Hammond (14 seasons; 1995–2009)

The consummate impressionist technician, Hammond came to Saturday Night Live and became the show’s premiere celebrity impersonator for more than a decade. Being older than his castmates and beset with myriad psychological issues (as outlined feelingly in his harrowing memoir, God, If You’re Not Up There, I’m F***ed) left Hammond somewhat isolated in his impersonations role, although he was certainly a valuable asset in non-impression sketches. Still, Hammond was astoundingly accomplished, his precise yet lived-in approximations of figures as varied as Regis Philbin, Al Gore, Donald Trump, Phil Donahue, Chris Matthews, John Travolta, and more genuinely marvelous.

Others, like his irascible Celebrity Jeopardy standout Sean Connery, are the uncanny product of masterful tinkering, with Hammond eventually stretching the real and the perceived into a shape as recognizable as the actual figure himself. Of course, a presidential impression is money in the bank for an SNL star, and Hammond’s Bill Clinton is both more precise and more subtly heightened than even Phil Hartman’s, with Hammond also scoring big by aping perennial public figures like Gore, Dick Cheney, and John McCain, all impressions with a high degree of difficulty. Leaving the show in 2009, Hammond has found his way back to Studio 8H as the replacement for the legendary announcer Don Pardo, who died in 2014. Naturally, during the waning years of Pardo’s reign, that was Hammond’s voice subbing in, without anyone being the wiser. —D.P.

Adam Sandler (5 seasons; 1991–1995)

In the comprehensive oral history of the show, Live From New York, former SNL writer and subsequent sketch comedy and dramatic superstar Bob Odenkirk said, not unkindly, of Adam Sandler‘s comic style on Saturday Night Live, “I think Sandler really seemed to take everybody by surprise. I mean, the things that Adam was doing were so sort of inconsequential — silly songs and just like basically dicking around, you know.” And, indeed, Sandler’s stardom came on the back of him dicking around with funny voices, childish characters, and sketches surrounding both. Recurring bits like Opera Man, where Sandler, draped in a cape, regaled Weekend Update with off-key, operatic renditions of the news of the day, weren’t exactly tight political satire. But audiences gravitated to the young comic in droves, with Sandler’s star rising the more airtime he got to take his performance-based silliness to even goofier heights.

During Sandler’s tenure, SNL infamously put out a best-of tape called The Bad Boys of SNL, highlighting the brash and often juvenile stylings of pals Sandler, Chris Farley, Chris Rock, and David Spade, among others, and, indeed, Saturday Night Live, for a time, became very much the high school boys locker room many of its critics had called it over the years. Sandler and Farley, while both still incredibly popular with audiences, were eventually fired in 1995 by Michaels, who was stung by the criticism. But both performers rode their SNL success to Hollywood superstardom, in turn validating the audience’s appetite for inspired silliness and knock-down, drag-out belly-laughs. —D.P.

Andy Samberg (7 seasons; 2005–2012)

It’s not every cast member who can claim their work both reinvigorated the show and introduced it to an entirely new audience, but Andy Samberg can. Filmed pieces have always been part of SNL‘s DNA, but when Samberg and his Lonely Island comedy partners Akiva Schaffer and Jorma Taccone made their mark with the trio’s Digital Shorts, it was truly one of the major landmarks for the show. When one of their earliest videos, the incongruously energetic rap between straitlaced white guys Samberg and Chris Parnell, “Lazy Sunday,” became a runaway smash on the then-nascent YouTube, it vaulted the Lonely Island guys onto what was their own fiefdom inside of SNL.

Inexpensive to produce (their first, the lo-fi and bizarrely brilliant “Lettuce,” reportedly cost $20) and consistently fresh and hilariously strange, the trio’s Digital Shorts became a mainstay on the program, even as Samberg flourished as a live sketch performer. (Meanwhile, NBC, in its rush to quash a good thing, initially sued to take down “Lazy Sunday,” only later recognizing that uploading sketches to YouTube was an untapped gold mine.) Samberg on live TV was an irrepressible mix of rubber-faced energy and utter commitment to the bit, with a sideline in creditable impressions, such as his uproariously out-of-touch Nicolas Cage, who repeatedly appeared on Weekend Update to suggest that his actual life mirrors the outlandishly awesome nature of his films.

Samberg came back to SNL as a recurring guest in its 50th season, playing Second Gentleman Doug Emhoff to Maya Rudolph’s Vice President Kamala Harris. Along with Samberg’s welcome presence in live sketches again, Lonely Island’s Digital Shorts returned (including “Here I Go,” featuring Charli XCX), familiarly amassing millions of views on YouTube. —D.P.

Maya Rudolph (9 seasons; 2000–2007)

As multifaceted a talent as has ever been on SNL, Rudolph brought consummate showmanship along with stellar musical comedy chops (her mom was singing legend Minnie Ripperton) and a mobile, chameleonic physicality to her time on the show. She could go big and brassy as a boisterous Oprah or spaced out and crooning Whitney Houston. She teamed perfectly with fellow female powerhouses Amy Poehler, Kristen Wiig, Ana Gasteyer, Rachel Dratch, and Tina Fey to carry the single most impressive women-led cast in the show’s history.

Rudolph — who appeared in three episodes of the 1999–2000 season before starring in seven full seasons and sticking around for a few episodes of the 2007–2008 season — donned innumerable wigs and accents to kill it as everyone from Italian American housewives to Liza Minnelli, and Beyoncé to Michelle Obama, all while lending each characterization a lived-in substance that was funny from the inside out. Another cast member like Hartman or Bill Hader who provided a reliably hilarious center to countless sketches, Maya Rudolph has found a second wind of appreciation in the 2020s with her Emmy-winning stint as Vice President Kamala Harris. —D.P.

Kristen Wiig (7 seasons; 2005–2012)

One of the most prolific performers ever when it comes to recurring characters, Kristen Wiig was so ubiquitous during her time on SNL that it’s tempting to discount just how popular and hilarious she was. Certainly, her army of broad, schticky characters (the Target Lady; mischievous grade school oddball Gilly; Dooneese and her baby hands; Aunt Linda and her inability to keep secrets; inept and self-involved game show celebrity Mindy Gracin; perpetual one-upper Penelope; and on and on) were overused, but putting such a bounty of guaranteed successes in front of Lorne Michaels is a recipe for such overexposure.

Apart from churning out the hits, however, Wiig was a fearless and nimble sketch performer and more than capable impressionist, seeing her virtually take over episodes with her sheer range. Even working among very strong casts during her seven seasons on the show, Wiig was a major star. —D.P.

Kenan Thompson (22 seasons and counting; 2003–present)

In the TV and sketch comedy business literally since childhood, it might seem inevitable that former Nickelodeon star Kenan Thompson would wind up on Saturday Night Live as his birthright. But Thompson, the longest-running cast member in SNL history, earned every bit of his undeniable stardom. Genial and boisterous, Thompson has matured into a show-anchoring Everyman, all while mastering a razor-sharp underplaying style that counterbalances his performer’s urge to go big.

SNL traditionally relies on the game show template far too much, but it’s a rare cast member who can turn the thankless host job into something on its own, with Thompson being one of the best at injecting intelligent weirdness into the bit. He can go uproariously big, as with Diondre Cole, host of the talk show “What Up With That?“ where Cole’s inability to abandon his love of the show’s theme song inevitably derails the very real and famous guests from speaking. His Weekend Update favorite Willie, meanwhile, makes the concept of smiling through the unthinkable uniquely funny, with Thompson’s indefatigable charm buoying us as much as poor Willie himself. Thompson has been the Hartman-like glue for innumerable casts over his two-plus decades on the show, his easy professionalism and charisma always being an invaluable asset. —D.P.

Chris Farley (5 seasons; 1990–1995)

In retrospect, one might say that Chris Farley took all the wrong lessons from Saturday Night Live. Growing up idolizing the show and especially original cast member John Belushi, the similarly Chicago-born Farley barreled into Saturday Night Live so amped up with the boisterous comic energy that made him a star at Second City that he promptly turned himself into the SNL wild man of a new generation. And Farley was wild, crashing through tables, cramming himself into ungainly costumes, and going full red-faced dynamo mode all in pursuit of every last laugh in the building. And he got them, with audiences taking to the baby-faced, burly comic with a passion seldom seen before or since.

If, like Sandler’s, Farley’s characters were loud, physical, and silly, the latter also brought along an unconcealable sore of self-doubt and childlike sweetness that could lend even his most over-the-top characterizations a twinge of affecting heartbreak. Farley’s most famous character, the overzealous motivational speaker Matt Foley, roared around his unlucky subjects’ living rooms, his blusterous badgering unable to hide Foley’s own aching awareness that he is, indeed, living in a van down by the river. And in what may be the closest approximation of the real Farley, his terminally awkward celebrity talk show host saw the flustered and sweaty cast member, as himself, simply wanting to ask his illustrious guests if they love the things they’ve done as much as he does. When the guests (namely Paul McCartney and Martin Scorsese) try to calm down the self-loathing host for losing his cool, their soothing assurance that Farley is doing all right comes across as the sort of deeply necessary balm he actually was always looking for. —D.P.

Dana Carvey (7 seasons; 1986–1993)

Anchoring one of the all-around strongest casts in SNL‘s history, Dana Carvey brought a bewildering array of characters and talents to his time on the show. As an impressionist, Carvey’s style was more, well, impressionist — his gabbling, discursive George H.W. Bush spinning out further and further while remaining resolutely tethered to some measure of loony reality (taking a similar approach for his recent recurring stint as President Joe Biden).

An inveterate performer, Carvey gave off a sense of perpetual people-pleasing, and the results were undeniably popular and hilarious, as the laughs echoed throughout his sketches. His Church Lady is one of the most imitated characters in the show’s history, Carvey’s years-long embellishment of scornful religious zealousness an indelible highlight. One of the few performers to ever overcome Lorne Michaels’ restrictions on ad-libbing, Carvey’s characters often sputtered and dithered so endearingly that his Paul McCartney or Ross Perot might overstay their allotted time, the audience’s delighted response taking the edge of Michaels’ irritation at his show timings being thrown off. —D.P.

Kate McKinnon (11 seasons; 2012–2022)

A comedy powerhouse in a precise, petite package, Kate McKinnon was the unquestioned centerpiece of Saturday Night Live for most of her decade-plus on the show. Sometimes, stars on SNL are born of effortful attention-seeking. Other times, you get Kate McKinnon, whose multifaceted talents simply expanded to fill out the show until she was the focal point for sketch after sketch. Although possessed of more political and celebrity impressions than almost anyone, McKinnon’s talents were never as much in verisimilitude as attitude, an unblinking channeling of character and moment that captured an individual as well as any expert impersonator.

Like any SNL star worth their airtime, McKinnon fashioned big, brassy characters for herself, from decrepit but plugging-away barfly Sheila Sauvage, and battered Hollywood trouper Debette Goldry, whose harrowing tales of old-timey sexism and abuse invariably shock present-day actresses into appalled admiration. Massive laugh-getters like Colleen Rafferty — whose unflappable response to the undignified alien abductions she’s subjected to — gave McKinnon license to be as knowingly gross as she wanted to be, while her political impressions (often as male members of the first Trump administration and, of course, Ruth Bader Ginsburg) gave her a chance to be bitingly topical and deeply silly all at once. Teaming with stellar castmates like Cecily Strong and Aidy Bryant was a constant and reliable recipe for excellence, with McKinnon proving an invaluable team player as well as a solo standout. —D.P.

John Belushi (4 seasons; 1975–1979)

While longtime creative partner Dan Aykroyd was never the superstar on the original seasons of Saturday Night Live that John Belushi was, it’s Aykroyd’s originality and writing skills from those first five years that have aged better. Still, there’s no debating that Belushi, a star at both Second City and the National Lampoon, emerged as the biggest star on the show at the time, especially after the premature departure of season 1 breakout Chevy Chase. Belushi was all about charisma, having learned through his time in Chicago’s Second City and onstage in National Lampoon: Lemmings that rock stardom and comedy stardom stem from the same, anarchic place.

Big and shockingly nimble, former high school athlete Belushi relished in physicality while displaying subtler acting chops when given the opportunity. Audiences were enthralled, eventually learning to explode in cheers and laughter at the simple cock of an eyebrow as much as an outsized pratfall or boisterous musical number. Teaming with Aykroyd conjured the duo’s Blues Brothers, a frenzied but precise amalgamation of the rock and comedy star, leading both actors to leave the show after its fourth season to pursue big-screen Blues Brothers success. Belushi’s time on Saturday Night Live was fraught and fruitful in equal measure, the brilliant comedian hurling himself into the backstage drama and onstage virtuosity with similarly bottomless capacity. —D.P.

Dan Aykroyd (4 seasons; 1975–1979)

His major hits (the Wild and Crazy Guys, the Coneheads, his endless parade of fanatical commercial pitchmen) left audiences bowled over, the irresistible weirdness and energy simply sweeping them along to wherever this young Canadian comic had in mind to take them.

Perhaps it’s the Canada in him, but Aykroyd’s unfettered imagination ran to staccato technical jargon seemingly culled from the world of David Cronenberg. How else to explain sketches like “The Blog Diet,” where Aykroyd’s narrator straightforwardly introduces the titular weight-loss program, involving subjects being kidnapped to a fake Arctic ice shack and being menaced by a food-hoarding Inuit man (Belushi) named Blog, who’s actually the professorial inventor of the titular diet. No one can. —D.P.

Will Ferrell (7 seasons; 1995–2002)

Hired after the mass exodus and critical and ratings desert that was the mid-‘90s SNL, ex-Groundlings alum Will Ferrell became one of the bright spots in a rebuilding season before catapulting into one of the most in-demand and reliably riotous performers Saturday Night Live has ever seen.

Ferrell’s stock-in-trade was a wide-eyed excitement that burned in even his most outwardly subdued characters. For instance: Placid suburban husbands suddenly erupt in strangled cries of “I drive a Dodge Stratus!“ in panicked defense of their own self-worth; a middle school music teacher maintains a singsong-performing delivery even as the boisterous indifference of his students rains down all around him; the carefully manicured persona of an overly handsy college professor explodes in thwarted passion from inside a bubbling hot tub.

Meanwhile, Ferrell brought us one of SNL‘s most memorable political impressions, his George W. Bush. While never the soundalike of his more impression-minded peers’ heads of state, it’s Ferrell’s adept channeling of the former president’s psyche and his confident touting of Bush’s “strategery” that has ultimately persisted in the public consciousness. Utterly fearless in his pursuit of huge belly laughs and possessed of a deceptively subtle actor’s delicateness when he chose, Ferrell was a scene-stealer in every one of his seven seasons. —D.P.

Gilda Radner (5 seasons; 1975–1980)

Almost every female cast member (and more than a few male ones) cites this original Not Ready for Prime Time Player as a formative influence, and it’s easy to see why. A hilarious combination of performing fearlessness and relatable vulnerability, Gilda Radner was as easy to love as she was impossible not to root for. Small and seemingly fragile, Radner specialized in hurling herself (sometimes literally) around the Studio 8H stage, matching and often outdoing her infamously boisterous and boorish male costars in how far she was willing to go for a laugh.

Once signing an end-of-year message to John Belushi by citing his ability “to hit me without hurting me and hurt me without hitting me,” Radner was every inch the dynamo on SNL her burly castmates like Belushi, Akyroyd, and Bill Murray were on a nightly basis, characters like her hyperactive child Judy Miller bouncing off the walls, and unshaven punk rocker Candy Slice spitting booze into Belushi’s unsuspecting mouth. Radner owned Update, correspondent creations like Roseanne Roseannadanna and Emily Litella becoming two of the most popular SNL characters of all time, while, in quieter moments, glimpses of the oft-troubled and lovelorn actual Radner imbuing her roles with an irresistible charm and melancholy. Radner’s shocking death from cancer at the age of just 42 in 1989 broke millions of hearts still touched by her sparkling and charismatic time on Saturday Night Live. —D.P.

Bill Hader (8 seasons; 2005–2013)

A beyond-worthy heir to Phil Hartman’s legacy, Bill Hader spent a similar eight years on SNL while displaying an astonishing versatility as an impressionist and serving a similarly indispensable role as the show’s go-to utility player. Thankless roles like ever-present game show hosts became, in Hader’s hands, the main attraction of sketches, with his ability to imbue potentially bland characters with hilarious inner life elevating everything he appeared in. Adding to that, Hader (who, in reality, suffered from debilitating anxiety on the show) was every bit the glue Hartman was, his precise and steady comic rhythm and timing the unwavering metronome that sketch after sketch played along to.

Even more than Hartman, though, Hader’s impressionist skills were unparalleled. The actor honed impersonations of figures from the ubiquitous (James Carville, Al Pacino) to the more inspired (Dateline’s Keith Morrison, Alan Alda, John Malkovich, Vincent Price), which were always guaranteed showstoppers both for verisimilitude and for the strange and wonderful places Hader would take them. Original characters like Weekend Update standout Stefon (co-created with pal John Mulaney, whose last-minute cue card switches invariably broke Hader on-air), cantankerous news reporter Herb Welch, and faux-Italian-babbling interviewer Vinny Vedecci own the rare distinction of successful recurring SNL characters who never wore out their welcome. —D.P.

Bill Murray (4 seasons; 1977–1980)

Arguably the most talented and accomplished comedian and actor to emerge from Saturday Night Live in the years since he left the show, Bill Murray came within a whisker of being one of SNL‘s also-rans. Brought in after Chevy Chase’s departure, the raw, young, Chicago-born Murray was shockingly shaky in retrospect, blowing lines and soon relegated to what he called “second cop” parts in the few sketches he appeared in.

Luckily, a bit of ingenuity and a lot of desperation (and a microphone-shaped bar of soap) saw Murray channel the confidently ironic wiseass within in the “Shower Mic” sketch, where an embryonic iteration of his soon-to-be-beloved Nick the Lounge Singer crooned to himself and Gilda Radner’s annoyed wife during their morning shower. The bit showed what the fiercely energetic and charismatic Murray could do, and, almost literally from that moment on, SNL viewers latched onto Murray’s signature mix of smirking silliness and performing courage.

In his short tenure on the show (before decamping along with Lorne Michaels and the rest of the cast after the fifth season), Murray exhibited a knowingness that turned his sketches into winking star vehicles. Originally auditioning for the show with a slurring, punch-drunk character he called “the Honker,” Murray relished in the looseness of scene work and improvisation, skills that often chafed against the restrictions of live TV, but nonetheless lent Murray’s characters an edge of dangerous agency that was consistently arresting. Amidst all of Murray’s stellar turns on the show, his resurrected Honker in the Tom Schiller-directed short, “Perchance to Dream” hinted most feelingly at the depth and breadth of Murray’s successes to come. Finding a bottle of booze on the snowy street, Murray’s Honker swills it down to imagine himself reciting Shakespeare to an adoring crowd, only to reemerge at the end of a cop’s nightstick, the tour de force a haunting omen of all that Murray had yet to accomplish. —D.P.

Get your daily dose of entertainment news, celebrity updates, and what to watch with our EW Dispatch newsletter.

Phil Hartman (8 seasons; 1986–1994)

Castmates coined the nickname “Glue” for invaluable Everyman Phil Hartman, citing the actor’s ability to ground and bring together even the shakiest of premises with his consummate, unflappable professionalism. An expert mimic as well as the sort of character actor a sketch show absolutely must have to succeed, Hartman was an older hire than the traditional new cast member, his years of work with L.A. sketch institution the Groundlings leaving him something of a steadying presence, even as Hartman’s versatility routinely produced some of the show’s most memorable and hilarious characters.

The wry manipulation of his “Unfrozen Caveman Lawyer“ revolves entirely around Hartman’s characterization, while the actor slipped in and out of celebrity impressions and original characters alike with a knowing and seemingly effortless brilliance. While other, younger cast members came and went, Hartman was just everywhere, doing everything. From game show hosts, old-timey movie types, interviewers, and persnickety chefs, to Bill Clinton, Frank Sinatra, Ronald Reagan, and Donald Trump, Phil Hartman indeed held Saturday Night Live together with his extraordinary talent. —D.P.

Eddie Murphy (4 seasons; 1980–1984)

The only person from the Dick Ebersol-produced years of the show to make this list, time and a string of disappointing career choices may have dulled the shine on Eddie Murphy‘s superstardom on Saturday Night Live. However, go back and watch — from the first moment Murphy, then all of 19, stepped in front of the cameras, audiences were enraptured. Impossibly young, sparklingly talented, with a potent mix of rawness and innate performer’s charisma, Murphy emerged from the rubble that was the initial post-Lorne Michaels SNL and built himself a one-man comedy empire, right in Studio 8H.

Originally paired with Joe Piscopo, one of the only other performers to survive the infamously disastrous 1980 Jean Doumanian-produced season, the more experienced Piscopo and newcomer Murphy indeed made a fine team, their chemistry propping each other up as they crafted some funny characters amidst the chaff. But Piscopo had a ceiling, while Murphy had seemingly none, with the younger star inevitably eclipsing not just his friend and scene partner, but at times the show itself.

The lore of those years is rife with tales of how it was emerging star Murphy who literally saved the show from cancellation on multiple occasions, his stable of larger-than-life guaranteed hits (Buckwheat, Gumby, Mister Robinson, and others) ever emerging to rapturous response. That said, backstage, the still shockingly young Murphy was a true team player. According to stalwart supporting player Tim Kazurinsky in the documentary Saturday Night Live in the ‘80s: Lost & Found, the unquestioned star was also “a mensch,” who fought to include his costars in sketches and gave his all in roles where he wasn’t the main focus.

As talented as Murphy was, movies came calling, with the actor immediately taking over the box office in films like 48 Hrs. (1982), Trading Places (1983), Beverly Hills Cop (1984), and Coming to America (1988), all while his stand-up career exploded in similar fashion. After leaving SNL in 1984, Murphy’s career had its ups and downs, with a joke about the latter from David Spade on Weekend Update reportedly causing a schism between the actor and show that would only be healed when Murphy returned to triumphantly host in 2019. —D.P.

news.title: Map Shows Democrat, Republican Voter Registration Shifts 38 Days to Midterm
news.text: Democrats have cut into Republicans' voter registration advantage in several states with competitive Senate races ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, though Republicans retain advantages in some of the conservative states that appear increasingly competitive. The race for Senate control appears increasingly competitive ahead of the November 3 elections, with Democrats leading some polls in more conservative states like Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas, all of which backed President Donald Trump by double digits in 2024. Democrats are increasingly hopeful that they can expand the electoral battleground to compete in these states that have historically been more difficult. This is largely due to Trump’s approval rating falling to new lows in polling this week amid frustrations with the economy, cost of living and soaring gas prices amid the Iran war. Voter registration data can reveal changes in states’ partisan composition, but it’s not always predictive of how a state will vote, particularly during a wave year when one party is benefiting from a strong national environment. These numbers can be influenced by factors including population shifts, migration patterns, the removal of inactive voters from voter rolls and people leaving a party when they are dissatisfied with its direction. Notably, not all states have registration by party. Georgia, Michigan, Minnesota, Ohio and Texas all have fairly competitive races this year, but there is no partisan registration in those states. Stephen Farnsworth, political science professor at the University of Mary Washington, told Newsweek that voters “often punish the president’s party in midterm elections.” Trump’s unusually low approval rating is making things worse for Republicans compared to the usual midterm pain for the party in the White House, he said. “Angry voters are more engaged as shown in the latest registration figures. A lot of young people in particular worry about the availability of good jobs in the face of growing AI, which is another policy area where Trump is out of step with voters,” Farnsworth said. Where Democrats Are Gaining There are several states where Democrats have narrowed the gap in voter registration that also have competitive Senate races this year, though Republicans do hold advantages in each of these states. Alaska The gap has slightly narrowed in Alaska, where GOP Senator Dan Sullivan is facing a challenge from former Representative Mary Peltola. In December 2025, Republicans had a 73,829 advantage on the voter rolls. That had narrowed to a 72,290-voter advantage in September 2026, according to the Alaska Division of Elections. Polls show a tight race in the state, which backed Trump by about 13 points in the 2024 election. Alaska has been viewed as a reliably Republican stronghold, but a leftward shift in cities like Anchorage has loosened the GOP’s grip on the state. The latest Alaska Survey Research poll showed a tight race, with Peltola leading Sullivan in the final round of ranked-choice, 50.6 percent to 49.4 percent. It surveyed 1,495 likely voters from August 20 to 23 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. Peltola had a larger lead in a poll from Data for Progress, which surveyed 578 likely voters July 28-August 4. It showed Peltola up 6 points, 53 percent to 47 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. However, a poll from The New York Times and Siena University, conducted among 593 likely voters June 15-29, showed Sullivan up 2 points, 47 percent to 45 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.9 percentage points. The Cook Political Report classifies the race as a toss up. Newsweek reached out to the Peltola and Sullivan campaigns for comment via email. Iowa In Iowa, a former battleground that has become more conservative over the past decade, Democrats have also been able to chip away at Republicans’ advantage. In December 2025, there were 196,755 more Republicans than Democrats in Iowa. As of September 2026, that number was 182,715. Iowa also backed Trump by about 13 points in 2024, as Republicans have made gains among the state’s rural, white population. Democrats have failed to make up those losses in suburban areas around cities like Des Moines. But the Senate race between Republican Representative Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Representative Josh Turek appears competitive. A new poll from Marist University gave Turek an 8-point advantage, 50 percent to 42 percent. It surveyed 1,050 registered voters from September 17 to 20, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. However, Hinson led the latest survey from co/efficient by 4 points, 46 percent to 42 percent. It surveyed 831 likely voters from September 14 to 16, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.39 percentage points. Turek also led Hinson in a recent YouGov poll. He had a single-point lead, 44 percent to 43 percent, among registered voters, but led by 4 points, 47 percent to 43 percent, among "strict” likely voters. The poll surveyed 2,169 registered voters from September 3 to 8. Its margin of error was plus or minus 3.5 percent among registered and likely voters. The Cook Political Report classifies the race as a toss up. Newsweek reached out to the Hinson and Turek campaigns for comment via email. Kansas The Kansas Senate race appears increasingly competitive, with the Cook Political Report this week shifting it from Likely Republican to Leans Republican. Republicans have a sizable advantage of 394,642 voters in Kansas, down from 401,710 in November 2025, according to the Kansas secretary of state office. The Sunflower State backed Trump by 16 points in 2024. But it does have a Democratic governor, and suburban areas around Kansas City have narrowed Republican margins in statewide contests. Republican Senator Roger Marshall is up for reelection and is facing Democrat Adam Hamilton, a pastor. A recent poll from Emerson College was a statistical tie, with Hamilton receiving 45 percent and Marshall 43 percent. It surveyed 750 likely voters from September 15 to 16, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. A co/efficient poll also pointed to a close race, giving Marshall a 5-point lead, 49 percent to 44 percent. It surveyed 915 likely voters from September 8 to 10, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.22 percentage points. Newsweek reached out to the Hamilton and Marshall campaigns for comment via email. Nebraska Republican Senator Pete Ricketts is facing a challenge from independent candidate Dan Osborn in Nebraska. Osborn has said he would not caucus with either party in Washington, but he will need strong support from Democrats and independents, as well as some moderate Republicans, to win in November. There are 292,049 more registered Republicans than Democrats in Nebraska, down from 294,750 in 2025, according to the Nebraska secretary of state office. Nebraska voted for Trump by more than 20 points in 2024. Forecasters give Ricketts an advantage, with the Cook Political Report rating the race as Likely Republican. Polls show a close race. A SurveyUSA poll showed Osborn up 4 points, 46 percent to 42 percent. It surveyed 503 likely voters from September 8 to 13, with a credibility interval of plus or minus 6.4 percentage points. An Impact Research poll, an Osborn internal, showed an even race, each receiving 47 percent of the vote. It surveyed 600 likely voters from August 9 to 13, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. It was first reported by The Omaha World Herald. Newsweek reached out to the Osborn and Ricketts campaigns for comment via email. New Hampshire Republicans also have an advantage in New Hampshire, though it backed former Vice President Kamala Harris by about 3 points in 2024. Independent voters are key to the Granite State, viewed as having a moderate electorate with a libertarian streak. Republicans have a 43,022-voter registration advantage in the state, down from a 49,635 advantage in 2025, according to the New Hampshire secretary of state office. The Senate race between Representative Chris Pappas and former Senator John Sununu is viewed as a toss-up by the Cook Political Report as polls suggest a closely divided electorate. The latest survey from InsiderAdvantage showed Pappas up 8 points, 48 percent to 40 percent. It polled 1,200 likely voters from September 16 to 17, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. A survey from GOP pollster Fabrizio, Lee & Associates showed the race in a statistical tie, with Sununu receiving 37 percent support and Pappas 36 percent. Other candidates received less than 4 percent support, while 23 percent were undecided about who they would vote for. Another poll from the University of New Hampshire poll similarly showed Sununu with a lead, 45 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 1,878 likely voters August 20-24 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.3 percentage points. Newsweek reached out to the Pappas and Sununu campaigns for comment via email. Where Republicans Are Gaining There are two competitive states where Republicans have gained ground in voter registration. Maine In Maine, where Senator Susan Collins is facing a competitive race against Democrat Troy Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate, Republicans have gained a bit of ground, but Democrats still have an advantage on the voter rolls. Democrats had a 31,732 advantage in the state as of March, a shift from 43,755 in 2025, according to the secretary of state office. The Senate race is expected to be one of the most competitive of the midterms, with the Cook Political Report viewing it as a toss up. Recent polls pointed to a close race. A survey from The New York Times and Siena College showed Collins with a 3-point lead, 49 percent to 46 percent. It surveyed 619 likely voters from September 15 to 22, 2026. Another poll from the University of Massachusetts Lowell published on Thursday gave Jackson a 5-point lead, 48 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 650 likely voters from August 28 to September 14, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.66 percentage points. A Quantus Insights poll showed a statistical tie, with Collins at 47.1 percent and Jackson at 46.4 percent. It surveyed 644 likely voters from September 14 to September 15, 2026, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.3 percentage points. Newsweek reached out to the Collins and Jackson campaigns for comment via email. North Carolina Democrats have also lost ground in North Carolina, where former Governor Roy Cooper, a Democrat, is viewed as a favorite over Republican Michael Whatley. The Cook Political Report classifies the race as Leans Democratic. In 2025, Democrats had a mere 604 vote advantage. That has flipped to Republicans, who had a 7,403-vote advantage in the state as of September, according to the North Carolina State Board of Elections. Jeff Allen, a spokesperson for Cooper’s campaign, told Newsweek that North Carolina “is a 50-50 state,” casting the election as a “margin-of-error race.” “A Democrat has not won statewide federal office here in nearly two decades – and Whatley’s elite DC connections mean Republicans are going to spend whatever it takes to keep this seat,” Allen said. Newsweek also reached out to the Whatley campaign for comment via email. Polls have given Cooper a lead. A Quantus Insights poll showed him up 5 points, 48 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 686 likely voters from September 21 to 22, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.2 percentage points. Cooper led by 11 points in a YouGov poll, which surveyed 3,895 registered voters from September 15 to 18 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.5 percentage points. Cooper’s support stood at 52 percent, while 41 percent of respondents said they would vote for Whatley among registered voters. Democrats’ Chances of Flipping the Senate Farnsworth said that Democrats’ prospects “for taking over the Senate are better than 50-50.” “Voters struggling with high prices want to see a president focused on that issue and trying to do something about it,” he said. “Instead they see a president who promised a more domestic focus is stuck in an unappealing stalemate with Iran, with limiting press access to public events, and on building a new White House ballroom and a massive arch near Arlington Cemetery.” Prediction markets have recently shifted momentum toward Democrats for control of the Senate in November. As of Friday, Democrats had a 61 percent chance on Kalshi and a 63 percent chance on Polymarket of flipping the Senate. That marks a shift from one month ago, when Republicans had a 53 percent chance on Kalshi, while their chances were tied on Polymarket. Republicans had even stronger chances at the start of the year, holding a 68 percent chance on Kalshi and a 66 percent chance on Polymarket of holding onto the Senate. Prediction markets let traders buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real-money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always predict the future accurately. What Happens Next Polls will be closely watched over the coming weeks as the race for Senate control remains close. Candidates are making their pitches to voters across their states on issues ranging from the economy and foreign policy. news.title: ‘Prophet of Doom’ makes unexpected prediction about what Trump will do after presidency
news.text:
A man nicknamed as the 'Prophet of Doom' has made a prediction about what will happen to Donald Trump after he finishes his term as president.

Craig Hamilton-Parker is a psychic who has become well-known for his predictions about world events.

Over the years these have included things like the death of Queen Elizabeth II, who died in 2022 at the age of 96, as well as the coronavirus pandemic.

But now Hamilton-Parker has turned his attention to the US, speaking to VT.co about what the future may hold for Donald Trump.

One prediction in particular looks at Trump's future post-presidency, so what does Hamilton-Parker say about this?

“The key thing that I said that I thought was the strangest of all is that when he finishes his career as a politician, he will become a religious figure, religious-type figure,” Hamilton-Parker told VT.co.

He added: “And then we get this business with him dressed up like Jesus. And now we hear him speaking a bit like that as well sometimes. There's more and more of a sort of a ‘I'm here to save humanity’ sort of vibe to him."

Explaining how he gets his alleged visions, Hamilton-Parker said: "When it comes to you, you just get a feeling about it. I don't know, it comes out of the blue. It's like something just given to you.”

Hamilton-Parker even made the outlandish claim that Trump had been a Hindu priest devoted to Shiva in a past life who fell out of favour because of alcohol.

He said: “Which makes me think, was that past life? And did that past life bring kind of religious energy within him of some sort from India?”

However, other predictions that he shared with the outlet indicate that this may come later than many people might expect, saying that he predicts Trump might even serve a third term as US president, even though the US constitution limits people to two presidential terms.

Many of Trump's supporters continue to attest that he won the 2020 election against Joe Biden, claiming that the election was rigged, even though Biden won fair and square. 

If this were true though it would also mean that Trump was excluded from running again in 2024, where he beat Kamala Harris and returned to the White House.

Nonetheless, Hamilton-Parker said: “At the time of the next election in 2028, I feel - I've been saying this for a long time - that I feel that he will have a third presidency.

“There is so much going on in the world crisis-wise, and particularly with a war that will be, by that time, happening with China. So it's like, I have to take emergency measures, therefore I stay in control.”

Other predictions that Hamilton-Parker made involved dangers linked to artificial intelligence, more specifically that it would be connected to some sort of crisis in the financial sector.

It's certainly a rabbit hole to go down, but of course the only way to find out for sure what will happen is to wait and see - que será será.
news.summary: Craig Hamilton-Parker is a psychic who makes big predictions about the future

news.title: Kamala Harris is belatedly courting progressives. Is it too little, too late? | Arwa Mahdawi
news.text:
Does Donald Trump secretly want Republicans to get annihilated in the midterms? Because he’s certainly acting that way. He continues to brush off concerns about the cost of living, saying last week that high gas prices are a very “inexpensive price to pay” for the war on Iran.

And, of course, the president seems to have no plans to end that disastrous war, apart from making vague threats about blowing the entire country up. Trust me, he keeps saying, everything will get better after the midterms. But by the looks of his dismal polling numbers, not many people are swallowing his empty promises anymore.

Still, despite the mess the Republicans have made of the country, I wouldn’t feel too optimistic about the Democrats returning to power: the party is famous for snatching defeat from the jaws of victory. Instead of evolving, it has a tendency to do the same thing over and over again, expecting different results.

See, for example, the fact that there are once again loud murmurings that Kamala Harris plans to run for president in 2028. The former vice-president hasn’t made any sort of official announcement yet – she told voters in Detroit this week that she’s still deciding what to do – but she seems to be testing the political waters through midterm campaigning.

This week she flew to Michigan, one of the states she lost to Trump in 2024, to join the Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed at a roundtable focused on Black maternal health. Harris will also be campaigning with the senator Jon Ossoff in Georgia next month and attending an event in Las Vegas with the Nevada attorney general, Aaron Ford, for his gubernatorial bid.

Harris’s appearance in Michigan wasn’t some spur-of-the-moment attempt to be helpful; it was a highly calculated move designed to put her back on the national political stage.

The New York Times reported this week that Harris’s aides had circulated a donor prospectus in July “that showed how she would try to maintain her influence atop the Democratic Party as she considered another run for president in 2028”. The document, which solicited funds for campaign travel, explained how Harris could boost midterm candidates. It also asserted that the current moment is “uniquely suited to Vice President Harris and a broad coalition already in motion”.

But not everyone agrees it’s Harris’s time to shine. Numerous Democratic candidates have publicly stated that they don’t want Harris’s toxic brand anywhere near their elections.

El-Sayed, meanwhile, seems to have decided that an alliance with Harris is mutually beneficial. It gives the progressive candidate an inroad into the establishment and might help him win more support with Black voters.

Harris, who alienated many progressives and Arab Americans by her stance on Gaza, clearly thinks that associating with El-Sayed might improve her reputation among that cohort of voters. El-Sayed has said he opposes military aid to Israel and termed the situation in Gaza a genocide – as have numerous human rights groups and genocide experts.

El-Sayed isn’t the only progressive that Harris appears to be trying to build bridges with. Last year, Harris offered only the most lukewarm of endorsements for Zohran Mamdani, stating: “He’s the Democratic nominee, and he should be supported.” Now that it’s clear that Mamdani embodies the political zeitgeist, she’s a lot more keen to be besties. In early July, Axios reported that Harris called up the New York mayor a couple of days after three leftwing candidates he’d endorsed won their primaries over establishment-backed candidates.

In fact, Harris has been working the phones pretty hard. The same Axios piece noted that she’d reached out to a number of pro-Palestinian activists and Arab American leaders including James Zogby, founder and president of the Arab American Institute. He told Slate this week that the two had had a “long talk”, which he felt good about.

In 2024, the Democrats took progressives for granted. They assumed that young progressives would show up to vote blue no matter who, even when the party treated them with disdain. Instead many of these voters stayed home.

The Democrats are still loath to admit that Gaza was a factor in their defeat: a 2024 autopsy report released by the Democratic National Committee did not mention the issue once. However, it looks like Harris is waking up to the realization that her almost unconditional support for Israel hurt her in the previous election and is something she will have to rectify if she wants to run again. Particularly since polls show a record 60% of US adults now have an unfavourable view of Israel and the vast majority of Democrats support an arms embargo.

Is all this too little too late for the former nominee’s brand? I don’t know. But it’s certainly too late for the tens of thousands of Palestinians the Biden-Harris administration were complicit in killing.

The murder of nine women causes a reckoning in South Africa

The bodies of nine women have been found across the Ekurhuleni district, east of Johannesburg, over the past two months. Some were naked or partially clothed. The apparent murders, which may be connected, have reignited protests about the country’s femicide rate, which is five times higher than the global average. Hundreds of demonstrators marched through Cape Town on Thursday, demanding an end to gender-based violence.

Afghan cyclist who disguised herself as a man to train wins Asian Games silver

Fariba Hashimi was attacked with stones and had to train while disguised as a man when she first started cycling. Now based in Italy, Hashimi won an Asian Games silver medal on Tuesday and hopes to compete in the 2028 Los Angeles games.

A Republican senator has warned that furries are infiltrating the aviation community

“It’s terrifying when you think about this,” the senator Tommy Tuberville said this week. “When you walk onto a commercial flight, it’s possible that the pilot flying your plane could have a deranged fetish of dressing up like an animal.” Tuberville seems to be referencing an incident in April when pilots were heard making “meow” sounds over an air traffic control frequency at Ronald Reagan Washington national airport. Is it possible they were maybe just mucking around? Or have the friendly really skies been taken over by a dastardly coalition of furries?

Masked lesbian infighting went ultra-viral this week

I wrote about the Last Ditch drama here.

The dangers of AI are already here

“The future is already here – it’s just unevenly distributed,” the science fiction writer William Gibson once said. And that is very true of AI. “We don’t have to wait to see how AI will bring about unprecedented death and destruction, because we’ve already witnessed its unleashing,” Granate Kim and Mohamed Hussein write in the Guardian.

Six-year-old Chinese girl ‘sets new women’s Rubik’s Cube world record’

Lian Yunzhi is reportedly “the first female speedcuber to average under 4.5 seconds”.

A day in the life of a pregnant woman in Gaza

Sitting in her tent, warding off rats, Alaa watches videos of her three children, killed in an Israeli airstrike, on her cracked smartphone. She gave birth to a new baby boy, Waseem, shortly after the Guardian published this piece.

Ed Sheeran’s shows at Gillette Stadium canceled due to nor’easter

A hilarious development in the Ed “I’m not complicit in genocide” Sheeran tour story. Even the weather is sick of hearing him whine.

 Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist
