news.title: Abdul El-Sayed Gets Boost in Michigan as Voters Sour on AI Data Centers
news.text: As artificial intelligence and the data centers that power it become increasingly unpopular with voters, progressive Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed is cashing in on the issue in Michigan's U.S. Senate race. A New York Times/Siena poll released Thursday found that 46 percent of Michigan voters trust El-Sayed to handle AI and data centers, compared with 35 percent who favor Republican former Representative Mike Rogers. Voters are also skeptical of the technology, with 66 percent opposing the construction of AI data centers and 29 percent supporting it. El-Sayed's advantage on data centers is wider than his lead in the race, with the poll showing him ahead 49 percent to 44 percent among likely voters overall. Newsweek reached out to both campaigns for comment on Friday. El-Sayed Holds Lead in Top-Rated Poll The Times/Siena result is the second-largest lead for El-Sayed in any September poll. Only the Suffolk University survey released Monday, which gave him a 7-point advantage, showed a wider margin. The poll surveyed 605 likely voters in Michigan from September 15-22 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.9 percentage points. The partisan split is nearly complete. Only 3 percent of Democrats backed Rogers, roughly matching the share of Republicans who backed El-Sayed. Independents look different in this poll than in others. El-Sayed held a 1-point edge in the Times/Siena survey, while Suffolk had him ahead by 16 points with that group. Age is the sharpest divide. El-Sayed leads by 71 points among voters ages 18 to 29 and by 21 points among those 30 to 44. Rogers leads by 16 points among voters 45 to 64 and by 5 points among those 65 and older. Rogers' attacks appear to have worked on one question. Fifty percent of voters described El-Sayed as the more extreme candidate, compared with 36 percent who said the same of Rogers. Voters still gave El-Sayed the edge on being an effective senator, 47 percent to 43 percent, despite Rogers' more than a decade in Congress. Mike Rogers vs. Abdul El-Sayed: Latest polls in Michigan Senate race Most recent polls show El-Sayed narrowly ahead. A Suffolk University survey of 500 likely voters, conducted September 16-20, gave him a 47 percent to 40 percent lead. Earlier polls from The Washington Post and George Mason University's Schar School of Policy and Government, as well as CNN and SSRS, gave El-Sayed 3-point leads. Emerson College, InsiderAdvantage and the Republican-aligned Trafalgar Group each found a tighter 2-point race. Only one poll in the past month had Rogers ahead. The Glengariff Group gave him a 1-point lead in a late-August survey conducted for The Detroit News and WDIV in Detroit. Latest Developments in Michigan Senate Race The Times/Siena poll caps a strong stretch for El-Sayed. This week, Sabato's Crystal Ball moved the race from "Toss-up" to "Leans Democratic," calling El-Sayed a "soft favorite" over Rogers. Former Vice President Kamala Harris joined El-Sayed at a campaign event in Detroit this week. El-Sayed said he hoped to expand his coalition to include voters who backed Harris in 2024. The candidates have yet to debate. Rogers skipped a televised debate on Fox 2 Detroit last week, saying he "never agreed" to it, while El-Sayed spoke for an hour beside an empty podium. Rogers accused moderator Roop Raj of bias, a claim Raj rejected. Rogers said two televised debates are scheduled for October. Forecasts and betting markets have also moved toward El-Sayed. Decision Desk HQ gives him a 67 percent chance of winning, with its director of data science, Scott Tranter, saying that "time is running out" for Rogers to close the gap. Spending is climbing, too. Spending in the race is approaching the $222 million spent on Michigan's 2024 Senate contest. Six of the top 10 outside spenders this year are backing Rogers. Where Does Abdul El-Sayed Stand on Data Centers? El-Sayed has made opposition to data centers a central part of his campaign. He has called for state and local moratoriums on new facilities until federal rules require union jobs, prevent utility bill increases, protect water resources and fund power-grid investments. His earlier plan called for developers to guarantee no utility rate increases and pay for their own energy demands while requiring greater community transparency. El-Sayed has also used the issue to attack Rogers, accusing him of investing "up to $2.6 million...in the data center boom" while Michiganders face higher utility bills. When President Donald Trump criticized data-center opponents on social media in August, El-Sayed sought to link the president's comments to Rogers, saying Trump's position reflected his opponent's stance. Where Does Mike Rogers Stand on Data Centers? Rogers' position has shifted during the campaign. He initially avoided taking a public stance, declining to answer questions about data centers in January. By March, he said Michigan should compete for AI-related jobs and investment while arguing that data centers should pay for their own electricity so residents would not face higher bills. In April, he pointed to tax revenue from a proposed Saline Township data center and said it could help lower property taxes. In August, Rogers reversed course, telling The Detroit News: "I think we need a pause, probably." He later called for a one-year moratorium on new data centers. The reversal came days after The Lever reported on Rogers' investments tied to the data center boom. The Detroit Metro Times also reported that the National Republican Senatorial Committee had warned that anger over data centers threatened Republicans in competitive races. Rogers' new position puts him at odds with the White House. In August, Trump said communities opposing data centers wanted to be "backwards and poor." Vice President JD Vance did not mention data centers during his Michigan visit that day. Data Centers Emerge as National Midterm Issue Michigan is one of several Senate battlegrounds where the fight over AI infrastructure has become a campaign issue. Newsweek found that eight of the nine closest Senate races, based on the Cook Political Report's ratings, are in states with at least one planned data center, according to the infrastructure tracking site Cleanview. Opposition to the facilities crosses party lines. In June, 64 percent of respondents to a Reuters/Ipsos survey said they disagreed with building data centers at the current scale and pace. An NBC News poll found the same share of registered voters would be less likely to support a candidate who backs building the facilities in their community. Democrats hold a modest edge on the issue. The NBC News poll found voters trusted them more on "dealing with data centers," 32 percent to 20 percent. One-quarter of respondents said they trusted neither party. On artificial intelligence more broadly, a national New York Times/Siena poll gave Republicans a 2-point advantage, within its margin of error. Republican leaders have taken notice. In a memo, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned that the issue had become "a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle." Rogers' reversal on data centers came days after that memo. "Frankly, any incumbent, Republican or Democrat, should be concerned about being tagged as pro-data center," political strategist Pete Seat, a former spokesman for President George W. Bush, told Newsweek. Veteran Republican strategist John Thomas said the backlash is about costs that hit households directly. "Voters are not asking Washington to surrender the AI race to China," he told Newsweek. "They are asking why their electric bills, water, and grid should subsidize a tech campus they never voted for." Hasan Piker Association Remains Wedge in Race El-Sayed has tried to draw a clear line between himself and left-wing streamer Hasan Piker without fully cutting ties to the podcaster, who hosted him nearly 100 times and campaigned with him during the primary. Most Michigan voters still don't know who Piker is, the Times/Siena poll found. Fifty-four percent of likely voters said they had never heard of him. Those who do know him mostly dislike him. Thirty-four percent of voters viewed Piker unfavorably, including 29 percent who viewed him very unfavorably. Just 6 percent had a favorable opinion of him. Rogers has made the association a central line of attack, part of a broader effort to cast El-Sayed as too extreme for Michigan. The poll suggests that argument has found an audience. Half of voters said "extreme" better describes El-Sayed, while 36 percent said it better describes Rogers. Forty-three percent said El-Sayed is too far to the left, and 44 percent said he is not too far either way. Voters in the poll also held a negative view of socialism, 57 percent to 26 percent. Seventeen percent of likely voters described themselves as Democratic socialists. None of this has cost El-Sayed his lead on the ballot. Voters said El-Sayed has good character, 46 percent to 39 percent over Rogers. They also said he would be the more effective senator, 47 percent to 43 percent. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Dave Siminoff.

I have been writing a lot about the AI controversy lately, and frankly, they haven't been my best-performing posts. If I cared more about "the algorithm," I would drop the subject and move on to other, juicier topics. 

But AI policies matter, and not just in the ways that the opposing sides of this stupid debate want you to believe. He was 100 percent wrong — since that prediction, demand for radiologists has gone up, as has their pay, because AI replaced a TASK, not a job, and tasks are merely steps toward accomplishing a goal that computers cannot do. 

God bless @JensenHuang for being a voice of reason. In 2016, Geoffrey Hinton said we should stop training radiologists b/c AI would "make them obsolete in 5 yrs, maybe 10." There are 28,700 in the US today, BLS projects 29,600 by 2035. We need an @OldTakesExposed but for tech pic.twitter.com/UjJzYJnSrY— Adam Singer (@AdamSinger) September 24, 2026

But the misallocation of resources and the upheavals in the job world are only one problem AI will bring. Others come from poor AI training, information control, handing powerful tools to bad actors, and dumbing down the populace by telling them to rely on AI to do their thinking for them. No powerful technology is an unalloyed good, and to maximize benefits and minimize harm, you have to start by understanding what is real and what is false. 

Airplanes are good. Flying them into buildings is bad. You don't give up airplanes to prevent the next 9/11; you develop systems to minimize harm and maximize good, and the only way to do that is to think about the entire picture clearly and creatively. 

Until recently, I mostly ignored AI because the use cases for me were minimal, and the most interesting consequences of its spread were limited to the societal psychoses it spawned. Now, I am actually interested in how it works, its potential uses and dangers, and its economics (given how the rapid development of AI and the mania surrounding it have distorted investment psychology), and, of course, the political battle. 

It's fascinating, and somewhere between 75 and 90 percent of what is said is complete BS, hype, or spreading FUD (fear, uncertainty, and doubt).

It's the internet bubble, Y2K, and COVID wrapped up into one big package. 

But as with each of those, there was a kernel of truth hidden within all the blather. The tech bubble was based on a real phenomenon — the growth of the internet, which really has revolutionized the economy and daily life; Y2K was a real but limited problem that was blown all out of proportion, making billions for people and scaring the world unnecessarily; and COVID was a real disease that killed real people, but hardly the danger it was made out to be. Plenty of flu seasons were worse, and hardly anybody noticed. 

The growth of AI presents real challenges and opportunities. The irony in the discussion is that the least responsible actors right now are the companies that the politicians are moving heaven and earth to protect, largely because a lot of venture capitalists have placed really big, really bad bets on their revenue growth projections. 

The real crisis they are trying to solve is that many people could get wiped out by a market crash and bond defaults. 

Data center projects, of which there are now trillions of dollars' worth of promised investments, are facing real challenges, and the bottom line is that massive loans and profit projections are based on entirely notional (and questionable) construction and sales. Most of the projected revenue increases at the big "hyperscalers" (Oracle, Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and xAI) are based on sales of computing capacity to Anthropic and OpenAI, neither of which right now has the actual revenue to PAY for what they have purchased. 

The insurance markets are skeptical in a way that lenders and especially equity investors are not, and I would bet that the equity guys are wrong on this one. 

I watched an interesting video by an AI investor who doesn't believe that it is a bubble, and he has an interesting yet flawed analysis (ignore the YouTube graphic that makes it look like he is predicting a popped bubble — AI has told Google that graphics have to grab attention, even if they are deceptive.)

His argument is simple: the demand for compute still exceeds the supply, and in that he is 100 percent correct. He just misses the most important point while proving that dot.com was a bubble, but AI is not: the demand for compute is based on giving it away. If you hand out lots of free or reduced-cost goods, of course people snap it up, even when it isn't that useful. 

How many tchotchkes have you picked up at a convention or fair that you toss in a drawer and forget? Pens with logos on them, or other doodads that you would never pay for? You pick it up because it is free. 

Most demand for AI is like that. It is given away, or sold at well below the cost of providing the service. The costs of providing AI are in the trillions, and the revenue is in the billions. That is not a business that can survive without massive inflows of money from somewhere, and that somewhere is investors, who are running out of patience. 

It turns out that AI has some real value, just not, for now, many trillions of dollars' worth. Maybe someday, but not soon enough to save OpenAI and Anthropic from collapse without massive help from somebody outside the VC world. 

Worse, cheaper, open source/open weight models are getting "good enough" to replace the "frontier" models for many use cases, meaning that the market is much smaller for them than predicted. Gobs of software companies are pulling back on AI spend either because it doesn't pay financially, or because they can use low-cost or free models to do the work much cheaper. 

Which gets us to Hillary Clinton, Reid Hoffman, the Democrats selling doom, the entire PR infrastructure pushing doom, and the grasstops campaigns to slow or stop progress. Lots of interested parties want to change the game, since they are losing it. 

Does anybody think that Hillary Clinton or Chuck Schumer, who were born before there was even the idea of a computer, understand the ins and outs of frontier models vs open weight models? Yet there HRC is, discussing the dangers of models not run by the top-tier companies, which are the only ones to have done actual damage. 

It's about money. It's about control. It's about saving investments. And it is about controlling people's perceptions of reality. 

Panic is the best way to short circuit people's skepticism and convince them to hand over all the money and power in the world to the Clintons and Hoffmans of the world. 

Are there real issues to contend with? Of course there are. Should we let Hillary, Barack, and Hoffman solve them? 

You decide.

news.title: Kamala Harris Tried to Explain How an Algorithm Works. It Did Not Go Well.
news.text:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris appears to be keeping the door open to another presidential run. If her recent appearance on "Off Air with Big Boy" offers any preview of the message, or competence, she would bring to a future campaign, Democrats may be preparing for another defeat. The alternative, of course, is worse: a Harris presidency.

When the conversation turned to artificial intelligence, a field that is advancing rapidly but remains dominated by widespread ignorance, Harris showed she belongs firmly in the latter category. Her confusion over what an algorithm is offered a glimpse of the limited knowledge base from which AI and technology policy could be shaped under a possible Harris administration.

🔥🚨 LMAO! Kamala Harris just tried to explain THE ALGORITHM, and it is NIGHTMARE FUEL“Suggesting I have no more interest because I’m looking at this yellow flower… as though my brain can’t handle the fact that there may be a pink flower.”Then she pivoted to collard greens.… pic.twitter.com/H56CHApWSy— The Patriot Oasis™ (@ThePatriotOasis) September 25, 2026

"There is a part of this that is about understanding that, you know, if you keep seeing the same thing over and over again, know that you are being targeted because you looked at it the first time, they're just going to keep sending it to you. Which means they're trying to dumb people down with the assumption that people don't have any interest beyond what they've already seen," the former vice president said. "Think about that." 

"Oh yeah, the algorithm," Big Boy, aka Kurt James replied.

"Right, but the algorithm suggesting, I have no more interest because I'm looking at this yellow flower. I'm only interested in yellow flowers. So here's more yellow flowers. As though my brain can't handle the fact that there may be a pink flower that I might be interested in looking at," Harris said. "And so part of it is understanding how the algorithm is manipulating us and figuring out how we're going to psych it out a bit."

If this is the kind of thinking behind technology policy, Americans should be worried. Harris turns a fairly ordinary feature of recommendation software into a sinister theory in which social-media companies deliberately make users less capable of thought. It mistakes a profit-driven engagement system for a scheme to infantilize the public, and provides a ready-made rationale for unnecessary regulation. 

That is not what the algorithm is doing. Platforms do not decide that a user lacks the mental capacity to enjoy a “pink flower” after expressing interest in a yellow one. They track behavior and predict what content is most likely to retain attention, because attention produces advertising revenue. Cynical? Often. Sinister mind-control plot? Hardly. 

Harris’s explanation also erases the user’s role. People are not helpless captives of an algorithm. They decide what to search for, whom to follow, what to click, what to finish, what to share, and what to dismiss. They can select “not interested,” seek out competing viewpoints, and stop treating a social-media feed as their entire information diet. Platforms can influence attention, certainly. They do not abolish human agency.

The former vice president then explained how she escapes the clutches of the evil algorithm: by leaning into some of her favorite tropes about connecting with minority communities:

“I do try sometimes. I mean, you know, I love to cook,” Harris said, before touting her prowess at roasted chicken, pasta sauce, and collard greens.

Guy Benson: Now it’s time for another Guy Benson Show “Benson Bite,” where we bring you the day’s most interesting interviews in a bite-sized package. For the full episode, visit GuyBensonShow.com or wherever you listen to podcasts.

Joining us now is the junior U.S. senator from the great state of Ohio, Jon Husted, a Republican. Senator, welcome back to the show. Great to be with you.

I want to talk about policy first and then get to some politics. There is a bill that you have written on this issue and this firestorm around data centers. I know the opposition is trying to make a lot of hay over this because, as the polling suggests, it’s a good issue for them. You’re trying to address some of those concerns. It actually had quite a lot of support among House Democrats in addition to Republicans, but Chuck Schumer seems determined to stop it because maybe it might actually solve something and deprive them of a political issue.

Tell us about what you’ve done and why you think the Democrats in the upper chamber are at least pretending to be against it.

Senator Jon Husted: Well, it’s called the Ratepayer Protection Act, and it would require data centers to pay for their own infrastructure and electricity, including generation and transmission lines. All of those things would be paid for by the data centers. The cost would not be spread to the ratepayers, and it would protect American citizens from higher energy prices due to data centers.

My bill passed the House–the exact version of it–by a vote of 417 to 3. Nothing passes 417 to 3.

We brought it over here to the Senate and tried to get it passed by unanimous consent. The Democrats blocked it. So now we’re going to try again to get a roll-call vote on this, and hopefully get it signed into law so that we can prove to the American people we’re listening to them, that we care about affordability, and we’re going to stop their electric prices from going up.

But Chuck Schumer has said that he didn’t like it, and I think he called it a fraud.

Guy Benson: Yeah, he called it a fraud. But as you said, it passed 417 to 3 in the House.

Senator Jon Husted: Yeah. Hakeem Jeffries voted for it. AOC voted for it. Two hundred and six House Democrats voted for it.

The fraud here is what Chuck Schumer is trying to perpetuate on the American people: that they actually care about affordability. Because they don’t if they block this bill.

Guy Benson: Yeah, which they’re doing, at least so far. Do you have a commitment from Leader Thune to get a vote on this, to force this?

Senator Jon Husted: Yeah, we talked about it earlier today. We’re going to vote on it next week, our final week before the election. We’re going to be able to say to the American people, “We’re fighting to lower your electricity prices.”

We’ll see if the Democrats want to make it a bipartisan victory or if they want to own the defeat.

I think it’s pretty common sense. If you’re going to endanger Americans on the roadways through your actions, then we’re going to cut off your highway funds.

And I believe we will get it. It’s going to be better than what exists now, but there are some issues that have been left unresolved.

One that I’m very concerned about is why I have my TEAM USA Act. It’s the number of non-American citizens who are populating these college rosters and taking scholarships and roster spots away from American citizens.

There are some Olympic sports and other sports–tennis, golf, hockey, soccer–where the majority or all of the student-athletes at these colleges are from another country. And they’re taking up roster spots for American citizens.

So my bill would cap it at 20%. We’re not saying ban it. I’m not for banning it, but we’ve got to look out for American student-athletes first. If you’re asking the federal government to get involved with this, we ought to look out for American student-athletes.

And so I’m concerned about this.

Many of them now show that you are trailing in your race to the former Democratic senator from your state, Sherrod Brown, who was defeated by the people of Ohio after a very long career in politics. If you don’t like the policies regarding your higher healthcare costs, your higher electricity costs, things like that, those are his policies. These are the things that he enacted.

Voting for a lot of the radical left-wing climate policies, he closed 23 power plants in Ohio. We used to be a net exporter of electricity. Now we’re a net importer, and it’s all because of him.

And he drove up the costs of so many things. He was for amnesty for 11 million people in this country illegally, gave them your Social Security payments, gave COVID checks, gave free healthcare to people who are not from this country.

And as Ohioans are remembering this about him during his 50 years in public office, they are going to say no to Sherrod Brown once again.

They defeated him two years ago against Bernie Moreno. We will ultimately defeat him this year.

Yeah, polls are close. One came out today that showed us tied. But look, this is September. I’m worried about November.

And once we run the campaign and remind people about why they fired him two years ago, I am confident that we will win this election.

Guy Benson: There is, though, a lot of frustration about the way things are going. Republicans said, “Hey, elect us and we’ll fix a lot of the problems that were caused by Joe Biden, Kamala Harris, and Sherrod Brown.”

And a lot of voters are saying, “Well, I don’t feel like the problems are getting better.”

How do you respond to that? Because you can point backward at him, and I think that’s a completely fair hit. I think he deserves to stay retired.

But you also have to convince people who are giving you and your party a shot–who are dissatisfied–a sense that actually things are going to get better for them. And they’re not feeling it, many of them, right now.

What’s the message to those people?

Senator Jon Husted: Well, in Ohio, we have the most jobs we’ve ever had in the history of our state and the lowest unemployment rate we’ve ever had in the history of our state.

So the growth side of things is going well in Ohio in terms of jobs and low unemployment rates.

Costs are still too high for people, but remember, they went up to 9% under Joe Biden. We’re trying to bring them down with food, fuel, and electricity.

Look, if you ask, “What are we doing about it?” That’s what my Ratepayer Protection Act is about. It’s about making data centers pay their own way, lowering electricity costs for residents, and I’m leading on it.

He was in Congress for 32 years. What did he do? He did nothing. He celebrated the expansion of data centers when he was in the Senate, did nothing to make them accountable for paying their own way. And now Democrats are trying to block me after I’ve been here for 18 months and I’m getting something done on it.

So look, the Democrats have been very obstructionist on fuel. The voters know we’re for lower gas prices. We’re the party of “drill, baby, drill.” They’re the party of killing the Keystone pipeline. They don’t want more production. They don’t want supply to meet demand. They want higher prices.

That’s part of their radical policy agenda. It’s not an exaggeration.

Guy Benson: I’m glad you’re making this point. Sorry, I just want to jump in because it’s such an important point. I want to underscore it real quick.

They are using and exploiting higher gas prices and diesel prices, which are a painful problem. I’m not disputing that. But they are jumping in to point at you guys and Donald Trump and say, “Look at this horrible thing.”

Senator Jon Husted: Less of everything. And they’ve always wanted higher prices so that people would convert to electric cars and do the other things that they want.

news.title: Does America keep electing the wrong spouse? Recent first and second ladies aced out their husbands in law school
news.text:
Long before their husbands were elected president or vice president, several of America’s future first and second ladies had already eclipsed them in the law school classroom.

Usha Vance was described as “50 billion times better” than JD Vance in a moot court exercise, in a recent Vanity Fair profile of the vice president which spoke to their former professors and classmates at Yale. Hillary Clinton was remembered as a relentless go-getter, while Bill Clinton rarely attended class. And when a professor was asked to compare Barack and Michelle Obama, he offered an unvarnished assessment: “She was better.”

While the sample size is small, the pattern is striking.

Only four first or second ladies attended law school, long a training ground for America’s political elite. Each met her future husband there or arrived on campus ahead of him. Again and again, people who knew them at the time recalled a similar dynamic: The women were the standouts, seemingly destined to play second fiddle to no one.

The pattern raises obvious questions: Did America elect the wrong spouses? What stopped the women from running and winning?

Political scientists point to several factors, including the male-dominated nature of politics, long-standing sexism and a persistent gender gap in political ambition. Men, research has found, are more likely than women to seek office — including when women have comparable or stronger credentials.

Marilyn Quayle, the daughter of Hoosier State physicians, began taking night classes at the Indiana University School of Law in the 1970s. There, she met and married Dan Quayle, the future vice president under George H.W. Bush.

The couple sat together in tax lectures, but Marilyn Quayle drove much of the discussion and regularly sought out the professor afterward, Time reported in 1989. Classmates nicknamed her “superwoman” for balancing family responsibilities with law school. While pregnant, she even induced labor early so she could take the bar exam.

That reputation endured as her husband rose through politics.

“To be honest with you, I was campaigning for the Senate one time, and someone came up to me and said, 'I went to law school with your wife.' And I said, yeah, I was there too,” Dan Quayle later said.

In 1988, the year Bush chose Dan Quayle as his running mate, The Washington Post reported that stories about Marilyn Quayle’s classroom prowess had circulated for years.

“Over and over, men and women who attended night law school at the University of Indiana in the early '70s say flatly that Marilyn Tucker – a bright, friendly, industrious young woman determinedly bound for a career – was smarter than her good-looking, somewhat lackadaisical classmate, Dan Quayle,” the outlet reported.

Hillary Clinton attended law school at roughly the same time, studying at Yale Law School in Connecticut from 1969 to 1973.

There, she met her future husband, Bill Clinton. The pair first spoke in the library after Hillary Rodham, as she was then known, approached him and said: “If you're going to keep staring at me, and now I'm staring back, we at least ought to know each other's name.”

Years later, several classmates remembered Hillary Clinton, a Wellesley graduate, as the stronger student out of the couple.

“Hillary was the first to raise her hand and almost always had the correct answer,” former Labor Secretary Robert Reich recalled. “I raised my hand fairly often but got it wrong half the time. Bill missed most classes.”

“When we were in law school, she was by far a better student than either Bill Clinton or me,” Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal told a local news outlet in 2015.

The trend continued with Michelle Obama, who graduated from Harvard Law School in 1988 — the same year her future husband began classes there. The two later met at Sidley & Austin in Chicago, where the future first lady, then Michelle Robinson, was assigned to mentor Barack Obama.

When asked to compare the two, their former Harvard Law School professor Charles Ogletree offered a blunt assessment.

“[Obama’s] wife should have been president,” he told TMZ in 2017. “He was great, too, but she was better…She could easily be president, but I don’t think she will.”

Usha Vance, the California-born daughter of Indian immigrants, was no exception. Like Hillary Clinton, she met her future husband at Yale Law School — and, according to those who knew them, outshone him there.

She was “pegged as the brightest student in the class of 2013, possibly even a future president,” Vanity Fair reported earlier this month.

One classmate called her a “rock star.” And a former professor recalled her dramatically outperforming JD Vance during a moot court exercise, telling the outlet: “I gotta tell you, Usha must have been 50 billion times better than [Vance] was at that assignment.”

The experiences of these four highly accomplished law students — all of whom went on to help elect their husbands — raise pointed questions about gender and political power. For one, why didn’t academic success translate into electoral victories?

Michele Swers, a professor of American government at Georgetown University, said that talents that prove useful in the classroom may not necessarily lend themselves to campaigning for and holding office.

“Bill Clinton had certain political skills that translated in communication,” Swers told The Independent. “Law school is trying to teach you to be very detail-oriented and, you know, write successful briefs, which are not always the skills of politics.”

Kathleen Dolan, a professor emerita of political science at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, pointed to a broader obstacle: the longstanding dominance of men in positions of political power.

“I mean, men are much more likely to be elected leaders in our country,” Dolan told The Independent. “They have always been more likely to be elected leaders.”

The United States, unlike 63 other nations, has never had a female head of government and only elected its first female vice president in 2020. Women, who secured the right to vote nationwide in 1920, hold only about 28 percent of seats in the current Congress.

Dolan, whose research focuses on women and politics, said the four women also reflect an enduring “gender gap in political ambition.”

“Men are much, much more likely to run for office than are women. And perhaps more centrally important is the fact that men are more likely to run for office than are similarly situated women,” she said. Women “don't see the value in, aren't interested in elected political office at the same rates that men are.” 

Even men with fewer qualifications are more likely to run than highly qualified women, she said.

Hillary Clinton eventually ran for president multiple times, while Michelle Obama has publicly made clear she has no interest in seeking office. Marilyn Quayle and Usha Vance never gave any indication of interest in throwing their hat in the political arena.

“Part of the explanation for that difference in political ambition is that women see a hostile political environment,” Dolan said. “They expect that they would be treated in a sexist manner.”

That expectation is grounded in reality. In 2016, Donald Trump frequently faced accusations of sexism, including for calling Hillary Clinton a “nasty woman” and claiming she “doesn’t have the stamina” to be the commander -in-chief. In 2020, when Kamala Harris was running for vice president, t-shirts sold online reading: “Joe and the H**.” 

The gap in ambition has not narrowed in recent years, at least at the highest levels of politics, Dolan said. And Americans have grown more skeptical that a woman will become president in their lifetime, according to Pew Research Center polling.

Still, Dolan said, women continue to make gains at other levels of government. “There are women elected to city council and as mayors and governors and state legislatures and Congress all the time and at ever-increasing numbers,” she said.
news.summary: Second lady joins the ranks of Michelle Obama, Hillary Clinton and Marilyn Quayle, who were all remembered by classmates and professors as more talented than their future husbands, Brendan Rascius writes

news.title: Early 2028 primary poll shows clear frontrunners for both parties
news.text:
With the November midterms only weeks away, some are already looking ahead as buzz around potential 2028 presidential candidates has grown, with new polling showing clear frontrunners for both the GOP and the Democrats.

In a new poll released Thursday, Sept. 24, by McLaughlin & Associates, a showdown between vice presidents could be in the cards, as former Vice President Kamala Harris and current Vice President JD Vance lead their respective hypothetical primaries.

Thursday’s poll is the latest 2028 presidential primary poll showing Harris and Vance leading, with other recent polls, including one by YouGov/Bowling Green State University, showing the prospective candidates ahead of their packs.

According to the poll, Harris leads among Democrats with 29% support. Her nearest challenger, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, came in with 12% support, with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg at 9%; 15% of Democrats polled said they were undecided.

Among Republicans, Vance leads with 35% of primary voters; the battle for second is closer, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio at 15% and President Donald Trump’s son, Donald Trump Jr., at 14%; 12% of Republicans said they were undecided.

The poll surveyed 463 likely voters from Sept. 16 to Sept. 22, according to McLaughlin & Associates.

Has anyone said they plan to campaign?

As of Sept. 25, no, but some potential candidates have already seemingly signaled their intentions ahead of 2028.

Earlier this month, Newsom spoke with CNN and said he would not run in 2028 if Harris decided to campaign for the seat a second time. The California governor made the statement during a fishing trip in Montana with CNN’s Jake Tapper, after the reporter asked about his presidential ambitions if Harris joined the race.

On the Republican side, Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas fueled speculation about another White House bid.

"It’s no secret that I want to be president," Cruz said in August on Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick’s podcast.

While Cruz signaled his potential to run, Rubio has sought to subdue speculation, although he did not completely rule out a campaign.

"I don't know what the future holds, but I have no plans at this time," Rubio said during an official visit to Colombia earlier this month. "I'm not a candidate for anything right now. And I’m 100% focused on my job, and I have to be because I have two jobs.”

Fernando Cervantes Jr. is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach him at fernando.cervantes@usatodayco.com and follow him on X @fern_cerv_.

news.title: Rick Jackson’s Chances Boosted Against Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia Race
news.text: Two polls show Republican Rick Jackson leading Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia’s governor race, which might come as a surprise given the current momentum of Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff. Ossoff, who has attracted speculation as a 2028 presidential candidate for the Democrats, has at least a 10-point lead over his Republican Senate challenger Mike Collins in both polls. Conversely, the governor’s race in the traditionally red state is leaning Republican—albeit by a small margin. Jackson leads the former Atlanta mayor 47.6 percent to 45.7 percent among 712 registered voters and 48.7 percent to 46.7 percent among 678 likely voters in a Big Data Poll released Thursday. Similarly, 45 percent of 3,447 registered voters surveyed in a recent YouGov survey said they would support Jackson over 44 percent who backed Bottoms. Just last month Bottoms had a narrow lead on Jackson in some polls, including a Quantus Insights survey, which gave Bottoms 46.4 percent of the vote compared to Jackson's 44.9 percent. In July, a Fox News survey put her at 52 percent to Jackson’s 47 percent. These were conducted by different organizations from the September polls so the comparison cannot definitely prove a shift in support, but it does suggest possible gains for Republicans, who will be wanting to hold onto an office they have held for the last 20 years. What Do the Polls Show About Jackson and Bottoms? Jackson’s lead in the Big Data Poll, which surveyed Georgia voters between September 21 and 23, is lessened to a one-point gap when taking into account how undecided voters answered which candidate they leaned toward. Some 62.4 percent chose Bottoms and 37.6 percent chose Jackson, leaving Jackson’s support at 50.5 percent and Bottoms’ at 49.5 percent. The survey reported a margin of error of +/-4 percentage points for both registered and likely voters. But YouGov gave Jackson a bigger lead in the end, with his lead growing to 47 percent, over Bottoms’ 44 percent, when it included only voters meeting its stricter likely-voter criteria—people who said they would definitely vote rather than probably vote, for example. The pollster, which carried out its survey between September 15 and 18, disclaimed a margin of error of +/-2.7 points for registered voters and 2.9 points for the stricter likely-voter group. What Do the Polls Say About Ossoff? Ossoff enjoys a bigger lead in both the Big Data Poll and YouGov surveys. Some 52.2 percent of likely voters backed Ossoff, compared to 41 percent who backed Collins in the Big Data Poll, while the YouGov poll found 51 percent for Ossoff and 41 percent for Collins. This 10-point lead drops to 8 points when YouGov applies its stricter likely-voter criteria. There may also be signs of support for Ossoff beyond his party’s base: 14.3 percent of respondents in the Big Data Poll who said they voted for President Donald Trump in 2024 backed the Democratic senator, compared with 2.9 percent of former Vice President Kamala Harris voters who backed Collins. In Big Data Poll’s hypothetical 2028 Democratic presidential matchup among Georgia voters, Ossoff led the field with 29.7 percent among registered voters, before Harris (29.7 percent) and California Governor Gavin Newsom (12.8 percent). Why Georgia’s Governor’s Race Matters Georgia has become more of a battleground state in recent years. While it has repeatedly chosen Republican governors, it backed Trump in 2024, and voted for former President Joe Biden in 2020. The seat is open because Republican Governor Brian Kemp, who won his first term in 2018 and was reelected in 2022, is not allowed to serve more than two consecutive terms, according to Georgia’s constitution. This election will decide whether his party retains the office Meanwhile, a Bottoms victory would make her the first Black woman elected governor of a U.S. state. The simultaneous Senate race could also have an impact on the national election in 2028—Ossoff winning a state Trump carried in 2024 could add to his appeal as a presidential candidate. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: John Fitzpatrick and Trevor Davies
news.summary: Republican Rick Jackson's lead comes despite the same polls showing support for Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff's re-election bid.
news.author: Jordan King

news.title: America's Most Popular GOP Governor Trails Democratic Rival: Latest Polls
news.text: For most governors who have topped popularity rankings for more than three years, reelection would look like a safe bet, but for Vermont Governor Phil Scott, holding on to his seat is getting harder, according to a new poll. A new University of New Hampshire Green Mountain State Poll, released Thursday, found the Republican governor trailing Democrat Amanda Janoo by 6 percentage points. Janoo had 49 percent support among likely voters to 43 percent for Scott. “Democratic nominee for Governor Amanda Janoo has increased her support significantly since winning the Democratic primary last month and is now in a statistical tie with Republican incumbent Phil Scott. Scott’s job approval rating has been declining in recent months,” the survey’s press release said. The poll surveyed 882 Vermont residents online September 17-21, including 835 likely general election voters. The margin of error for likely voters is plus or minus 3.4 percentage points. Newsweek reached out to both campaigns for comment on Friday. How the Race Has Moved Scott has comfortably navigated politics in what is considered a deep-blue state, winning reelection in recent years and consistently ranking among the nation’s most popular governors. But the outcome of the Democratic primary has become his biggest challenge yet to retain the seat. “For Scott to be able to survive, he certainly has a bit of a hill to climb,” said Sean McKinley, University of New Hampshire (UNH) Survey Center project director. The partisan breakdown shows where Scott's support has shifted. He wins 89 percent of Republicans and 53 percent of independents, but among Democrats, only 20 percent back him, while 73 percent support Janoo. In Vermont, trade appears to be one factor. The poll was conducted after President Donald Trump's trade negotiations with Canada broke down and both countries imposed tariffs. Seventy-one percent of Vermonters disapprove of how Trump has handled the talks, while 77 percent say they are concerned about the impact on the state. “There are concerns that trade conflict with Canada may disproportionately impact New England,” the poll’s press release reads. As the November midterm elections approach, partisan divisions are becoming more noticeable. Scott’s approval among Republicans has increased to 77 percent, up from 60 percent in July to its highest level. Among Democrats, however, his approval has dropped to 35 percent, the lowest recorded level. The Cook Political Report, widely considered the industry standard for nonpartisan race ratings, still rates the Vermont governor’s race as Solid Republican. “After a massive 52-point victory in 2024, Republican Gov. Phil Scott should easily win another two-year term in 2026,” Cook states. Sabato’s Crystal Ball, Nate Silver’s Silver Bulletin and Race to the WH also rate the race as Likely Republican. What Earlier Polls Said Earlier rounds of the same poll showed Scott comfortably ahead. In June, he led Janoo 42 percent to 27 percent, with 26 percent undecided. In July, he led 44 percent to 33 percent. But after Janoo secured the party's nomination, the race shifted. In the August 11 primary, Janoo won 49.1 percent of the vote to 46.6 percent for Aly Richards, the former head of the childcare advocacy group Let’s Grow Kids. Janoo’s victory helped close the gap with Scott by 17 points in about two months. Democratic leaders had originally hoped for a more established candidate. The party tried to recruit Attorney General Charity Clark, Secretary of State Sarah Copeland Hanzas and Treasurer Mike Pieciak to take on Scott, but all three decided to seek reelection to their current offices. America's Most Popular Governor The poll sits awkwardly alongside Scott’s national reputation. In Morning Consult’s governor approval tracker, based on surveys of registered voters conducted from October through December 2025, Scott had a 74 percent approval rating. That made him the most popular governor in the country for the 14th consecutive quarter. Just 19 percent of Vermonters disapproved of his performance in that survey. But the latest UNH poll offers a more recent snapshot. When asked to compare Scott with his New England counterparts, Vermont voters gave him a lower approval rating than Democratic Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey, Republican New Hampshire Governor Kelly Ayotte and Democratic Connecticut Governor Ned Lamont. He still ranked ahead of Democratic Maine Governor Janet Mills and well ahead of Democratic Rhode Island Governor Dan McKee. Scott has kept his distance from Trump. He has opposed the White House on several major issues, including its tariff policies and the deployment of the National Guard to cities across the country. Yet the poll suggests that distance may not be enough for Democrats who are voting against the Republican Party as a whole. That would be a sharp break from 2024, when Vermonters split their tickets on a large scale. Vice President Kamala Harris carried the state with 63.8 percent of the vote to Trump's 32.3 percent. On the same ballot, Scott won reelection with 73.4 percent to 21.8 percent for Democrat Esther Charlestin. Scott carried every county, including many towns that voted for Harris. His vote share was about 41 points higher than Trump's. What Vermont Voters Are Worried About Trade with Canada, Vermont's largest trading partner and its northern neighbor, is the clearest concern. After Trump's negotiations with Ottawa broke down this month and both countries imposed tariffs, 71 percent of Vermonters said they disapprove of the president's handling of the talks, including 68 percent who strongly disapprove. Only 18 percent approve. Crime linked to drug use is another concern. The poll asked about a proposed safe injection site in Burlington, and 45 percent of residents said such sites increase crime in nearby areas. Only 12 percent said they reduce it. Sixty-two percent doubt the sites do much to cut drug use, even though a majority believe they help prevent overdose deaths. Cost pressures appear throughout the poll. Seventy-eight percent of residents support taxing homes that are not their owners' primary residence, a proposal lawmakers are reportedly discussing as housing prices squeeze year-round residents. Voters are more divided on how to control education costs: 49 percent support Scott's plan to consolidate school districts and possibly close schools, while 39 percent oppose it. Those concerns tend to divide along party lines, which is a problem for Scott. The worries Democrats voice most, especially trade, are tied to Trump and the national Republican Party. National Environment The Vermont results line up with a broader shift toward Democrats six weeks before the midterms. An Emerson College national poll conducted September 21-22 found Democrats leading Republicans 53 percent to 42 percent on the generic congressional ballot. An NPR/PBS News/Marist poll found Democrats ahead 53 percent to 41 percent, with Trump's approval at 39 percent and his disapproval at 53 percent. Pollster Nate Silver's generic ballot average had Democrats up 8.1 points, the party's best position of the cycle. The same pattern shows up further down the ballot. Former Lieutenant Governor Molly Gray, a Democrat, leads Republican Lieutenant Governor John Rodgers 54 percent to 35 percent. Democratic Representative Becca Balint leads Republican Gerald Malloy 66 percent to 30 percent for the state's at-large House seat. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: Vermont Republican Phil Scott, the nation's most popular governor, trails Democrat Amanda Janoo 49 to 43 percent in a new poll.
news.author: Jesus Mesa

news.title: Renée Good's Mom Wanted Trump to Protect Her Family. Her Daughter Was Killed by ICE.
news.text:
The killing of Renée Good, who was gunned down on a Minneapolis street in January by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer, was a tragedy.

The fact that Jonathan Ross, the ICE agent who killed her, has not faced any accountability for his actions—firing his gun wildly through the window of Good's vehicle as she tried to flee a confrontation that ICE officers had initiated and escalated—remains shameful.

This week, that story gained a new, heartbreaking angle when Good's mother, Donna Ganger, testified before a Senate committee that is investigating fatal shootings by ICE agents.

"My daughter should still be alive," Ganger said, holding back tears. More than nine months after Good was killed, Ganger said the family is still struggling with "the total insanity of it all."

Then, Ganger offered a detail that manages to both reinforce and complicate the established narratives around Good's killing. She admitted that she is a registered Republican who voted for President Donald Trump:

"I voted for President Trump, under the impression that these agents were here to protect the citizens of the United States—innocents like our family and the others here—against terrorists, certainly not to accuse those here of being terrorists and take precious lives."

That last bit is a reference to the smear campaign that federal officials began in the hours after Good was killed. Then–Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem said Good had engaged in "an act of domestic terrorism" prior to being shot and killed. Days later, despite video evidence that undermined the claim that Good had tried to run over ICE officers, Vice President J.D. Vance doubled down on the "terrorism" claim.

As moving as Ganger's testimony this week was, I've spent the past few days thinking more about what was left unspoken. Her situation is a compelling, brutal microcosm of what many Americans are likely feeling after seeing the chaos and the violence of Trump's immigration enforcement tactics. Just last week, an ICE agent shot a Venezuelan man in Texas—at least the 21st shooting by a federal immigration agent during Trump's second term.

Each of those incidents leaves a mark on a family and a community, but Ganger's situation is more raw, more vicious—as if the "I never thought leopards would eat MY face" meme had sprung to life and sat down in front of a Senate committee. Surely, Ganger never thought the leopards would kill her daughter.

Mocking Ganger is the wrong response, however. It misses the bigger point. Her vote didn't directly cause her daughter to be killed—indeed, her vote for Trump had no bearing on the outcome of the 2024 election at all, since Kamala Harris won Minnesota's electoral votes.

The person responsible for Good's death is Ross, who recklessly pulled the trigger. The culpability also lies with Noem and others in the Trump administration who favored an aggressive, confrontational approach to immigration enforcement and who sent hastily recruited, poorly trained officers into cities where clashes with protesters were highly likely and violence was all but inevitable.

I hope Ganger doesn't blame herself for what happened to her daughter. She's right when she says that Good should be alive today—and that fact doesn't change because of how Ganger voted.

Even so, the rest of America can take some things away from this awfulness. First, those in power should heed her call for accountability when federal agents commit crimes. The federal Department of Justice has blocked state investigations into Ross and other ICE agents who have harmed people. That's unacceptable. More broadly, laws should be changed to allow victims of all police shootings to obtain justice.

For everyone else, some reflection is necessary. The awful circumstances that Ganger's family has lived through are a reminder that voting for the state to do violence to others is always risky. When the leopard is out of the cage, you never know whose face it will eat—all you can do is hope the targets aren't you or your loved ones.

Politics often seems like a reality show, something that happens somewhere else and to other people. Ganger's testimony this week was cutting evidence of how authoritarianism can get deeply personal in ways no one wants to experience.
news.summary: Donna Ganger's heartbreaking testimony to a Senate committee offers a vital insight into the vicious politics of authoritarianism.
news.author: Eric Boehm

news.title: Full List of Times Susan Collins Broke With Trump in His Second Term
news.text: Senator Susan Collins’ record of being an independent voice has become a central flashpoint in the Maine Senate race, as she faces a competitive challenge from former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, a Democrat, ahead of November's midterms. Democrats hope to tie Collins, a Republican, to President Donald Trump, who is unpopular in the Pine Tree State, arguing that she only votes against him when her vote does not count. However, Collins has pointed to numerous major votes in which she has sided against the administration on some of Trump’s top priorities. Maine generally leans toward Democrats, having backed former Vice President Kamala Harris by 7 points in 2024. But Collins has been able to easily win reelection in the past due to her personal popularity and moderate, bipartisan image. Whether or not Mainers still view her as independent in the Trump era could be critical to her reelection chances, so this has become a key issue for both campaigns with less than six weeks until Election Day. Jackson spokesperson Maggie Amjad told Newsweek that Maine voters “aren’t stupid” and “see the game that Susan Collins is playing.” “The vast majority of Collins’ votes—96% of the time—have been with Donald Trump. In the moments when it mattered, Collins sided with Donald Trump and Washington Republicans—including voting to confirm the justices who overturned Roe v. Wade and helping advance legislation that slashed nearly $1 trillion from Medicaid to pay for massive tax breaks for the wealthy. Susan Collins has spent 30 years in Washington selling out Maine and putting billionaires first,” Amjad said. Newsweek also reached out to Collins' campaign via email. How Often Has Susan Collins Voted With Trump? A report from CQ Roll Call found that Collins voted with Trump 95 percent of the time in 2025. The only Republicans with lower scores were Senators Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky, making her one of the least pro-Trump senators. Still, Democrats have noted she does vote with Trump most of the time, with Jackson hitting out at her voting record earlier in September. “It’s pretty clear to me that you can’t have it both ways,” he said. “You can’t vote with Donald Trump 96 percent of the time and then turn around and claim to care about working class families.” She has faced criticism from Maine Democrats over several votes. Her vote in favor of Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh during Trump’s first term was seen as a major turning point in her popularity among moderate Democrats. Maine Democrats have also criticized her for voting to confirm several judges they say are opposed to abortion rights. Other positions she has taken, including her support for the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act and her vote to confirm Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as Health and Human Services secretary, have also drawn scrutiny. Collins was seen as one of the most anti-Trump Republicans during his first term in office. She declined to support him in the 2024 election and voted to convict him in his impeachment trial after the January 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol building. She also voted against a repeal of the Affordable Care Act in 2017. When Has Susan Collins Broken From Trump? List of Times Maine Senator Voted Against Him Still, there are several instances where Collins has broken from the president. In addition to these key votes, she has also been critical of other parts of Trump's agenda such as his tariffs and proposal to send Americans $5,000 if Republicans win the midterms. She has also used her position as the chair of the Appropriations Committee to push back against some Trump priorities. Iran War When Trump first launched the Iran war in late February, Collins declined to vote in support of a War Powers Resolution that would have limited his ability to wage war on the country, writing in a statement that passing the resolution “would send the wrong message to Iran and to our troops.” However, she has become increasingly critical of the administration’s approach to Tehran and has voted in support of subsequent resolutions. In April, she said in a statement that the War Powers Resolution “establishes a clear 60-day deadline for Congress to either authorize or end U.S. involvement in foreign hostilities.” “Further military action against Iran must have a clear mission, achievable goals, and a defined strategy for bringing the conflict to a close. I voted to end the continuation of these military hostilities at this time until such a case is made,” she wrote. The Iran war has become increasingly unpopular. Only 24 percent of Americans believe going to war with Iran was the “right decision,” according to a new YouGov poll, which surveyed 1,401 registered voters from September 18 to 21. That unpopularity is compounded by the rising gas prices, which stem from disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz, a critical passageway for the global oil supply. Gas prices averaged $4.492 per gallon nationwide and $4.431 in Maine as of Friday, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA). One Big Beautiful Bill Collins also voted against the One Big Beautiful Bill, a landmark piece of legislation for the Trump administration, citing concerns about its “harmful impact” on Medicaid. She said at the time she supports other tax relief measures in the bill. “This bill has additional problems. The tax credits that energy entrepreneurs have relied on should have been gradually phased out so as not to waste the work that has already been put into these innovative new projects and prevent them from being completed. The bill should have also retained incentives for Maine families who choose to install heat pumps and residential solar panels,” she said at the time. However, her vote on the bill has become a contentious issue. She has faced attacks from Democrats, who point out that she did vote to move the package forward in a procedural vote. Democrats have cast her vote as being critical in advancing the bill. The Maine Democratic Party wrote in an October 2025 statement that it was “another reminder of how Collins will always put her party’s interests ahead of Mainers.” Rescissions Collins also voted against advancing a rescissions package backed by the Trump administration that canceled billions of dollars in federal funding including foreign aid and support for public media like PBS and NPR. She said the text provided by the administration offered too few details and did "not give an accounting of the specific program cuts that would total $9.4 billion." “The rescissions package has a big problem–nobody really knows what program reductions are in it. That isn’t because we haven’t had time to review the bill. Instead, the problem is that OMB [Office of Management and Budget] has never provided the details that would normally be part of this process," she said. She also said she opposed "excessive cuts" to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting. Pete Hegseth Collins voted against the confirmation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, writing in a statement that she was “concerned that he does not have the experience and perspective necessary to succeed in the job.” “I am concerned that Mr. Hegseth does not have the management experience and background that he will need in order to tackle these difficulties. His limited managerial experience involved running two small non-profit organizations that had decidedly mixed results,” she wrote in a statement. Todd Blanche Collins also voted against the nomination of Attorney General Todd Blanche, pointing to what she viewed as an “increasingly political” Department of Justice during the Trump administration. “Mr. Blanche has taken several actions that have further eroded the Department’s independence, and that is the basis for my vote to oppose his confirmation,” she wrote. She specifically pointed to the anti-weaponization fund, designed to compensate people who claimed they were unfairly targeted by government investigations, as being key to her opposition to his nomination. The $1.7 billion fund drew criticism from Collins and other moderate Republicans. Kash Patel Collins also opposed FBI Director Kash Patel’s nomination, raising issue with whether he could be “decidedly apolitical.” “While Mr. Patel has had 16 years of dedicated public service, his time over the past four years has been characterized by high profile and aggressive political activity. Mr. Patel has made numerous politically charged statements in his book and elsewhere discrediting the work of the FBI, the very institution he has been nominated to lead,” Collins said. She was also critical of other Trump picks whose nominations were ultimately pulled, such as Casey Means, his nominee to serve as surgeon general. What Is Susan Collins and Donald Trump's Relationship? Trump and Collins have never been particularly closely aligned. She has said she did not vote for him in 2016 and 2024, and she did vote to impeach him in 2021. Collins is generally seen as a more moderate Republican than Trump. She has frequently opposed his measures, beyond just voting against him on major GOP bills. This week, Collins spoke out against what she views as an effort to politicize federal health research funding, after the Washington Post reported that Trump was considering an executive order to create a commission to review National Institutes of Health (NIH) grants. "The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) should not be involved in agency decisions on the awards of grants," Collins wrote on X. Vice President JD Vance in May during remarks in Maine said he is at times “frustrated” with Collins but acknowledged that a more partisan Republican may not win in a blue-leaning state like Maine. "The thing I love about Susan is she is independent, because Maine is an independent state, and frankly, if she was as partisan as I sometimes wish that she was, she would not be a good fit for the people of Maine," he said. "So, let's give a shoutout to Susan Collins, who is doing a great job." Susan Collins vs. Troy Jackson: Where Polls Stand Polls have shown a close race between Collins and Jackson. A new poll from The New York Times, The Portland Press Herald and Siena University released on Thursday showed Collins up 3 points, 49 percent to 46 percent. It surveyed 619 likely voters from September 15 to 22. But two other polls also released Thursday showed Jackson with a lead over Collins. Jackson led by 4 points in a new University of New Hampshire poll, which had him at 51 percent support to Collins’ 47 percent, an improvement from July when he led by 3 points. It surveyed 1,312 likely voters from September 17 to 21 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.7 percentage points. Another poll from the University of Massachusetts Lowell gave Jackson a 5-point lead, 48 percent to 43 percent. Among independent voters, a critical voting bloc in the Pine Tree State, he led by 8 points, 40 percent to 32 percent, with 22 percent still undecided, the poll found. Latest Developments in the Maine Senate Race This week, the Maine Senate race was rocked by a new report from ProPublica about alleged interactions between Collins and a major campaign donor. The FBI sought to launch a probe into Collins' dealings with a major donor, according to a ProPublica report, and the effort was abandoned after Trump's return to office, according to an investigation by the outlet. Collins’ office denied the report. Annie Clark, who serves as Collins’ deputy chief of staff, said the claims are “categorically false.” “There have never been any allegations of wrongdoing by the Collins for Senator campaign, and the campaign was never the target of the FBI investigation,” she wrote. Jackson responded to the report in a statement provided to Newsweek, accusing Collins of “corruption of the highest order.” “Susan Collins doesn’t care that we’re losing our health care, that ICE is killing people on the streets, and that we’ve been dragged into a pointless war—as long as her donors get their contracts and her coffers get filled. We deserve answers about every contract and every conversation that Collins and her team facilitated on the backs of taxpayers,” he wrote. “The jig is up.” Why the Maine Senate Race Matters in the 2026 Midterms Democrats’ path to a Senate majority runs through Maine. Democrats are increasingly hopeful about winning the Senate despite a difficult map. Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, so Democrats must flip four seats to win control if they win every race in a seat they currently hold. Vance serves as the tiebreaker in a split Senate. In order to flip the Senate majority, Democrats have to win every seat they currently hold, flip GOP-held seats in competitive states and win some seats in more traditionally conservative territory. Democrats are defending seats in Trump-won states Georgia and Michigan. In addition to Maine, they view a GOP-held seat in North Carolina as a top flip opportunity. The race in New Hampshire, which backed Harris by about 3 points, is also competitive. No other Senate races are in Harris-won or single-digit Trump states, meaning Democrats must expand the Senate battleground and compete in more conservative areas if they want to win the majority. They are targeting GOP-held seats in Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas as potential states to flip. The Cook Political Report classifies those four races as tossups. What Happens Next The Maine Senate race is expected to remain one of the most competitive battlegrounds of this year’s midterms, with forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball classifying it as a pure toss-up. Both candidates are likely to spend the coming weeks traversing the state to make their pitches to voters in hopes of winning over independent and undecided voters, while also motivating their bases to turn out. news.summary: Collins' independence from Trump has become a key question in her reelection bid against Democrat Troy Jackson in Maine.

news.title: Ex-Dem insider blows lid off fundraising 'gimmicks' during 2024 election: 'Pyramid scheme'
news.text: Lindy Li, a former Democratic fundraiser who switched her party affiliation over unheeded warning signs of President Joe Biden’s decline in the 2024 election, believes the party badly misallocated its fundraising, misled donors and rewarded party operatives who propped up Biden’s image. "It was: ‘maintain this very obvious lie in return for access,’" Li recalled in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, referring to assertions that Biden was not experiencing cognitive decline. "And whoever maintained, whoever was most strident in propounding that lie got the most access. And whoever subverted it or dared to ask questions would see their access quickly diminish." Li herself would find her access completely cut off after she began questioning Biden’s physical ability to serve another four years as president. But before leaving, Li became a top operative and is now chronicling the months leading up to Biden's withdrawal from the race in her new book, "Unburdened." Her revelations include what then-Vice President Kamala Harris did with a historic, billion-dollar war chest. NANCY PELOSI DENIES KNOWING ABOUT BIDEN'S DECLINE, CLAIMS THOSE WHO KNEW 'SHOULD HAVE ACTED' For starters, Li believes that the numbers themselves weren’t what they appeared to be from the outside. "I sincerely believe it's a pyramid scheme," Li said. She explained how fundraisers would sometimes take credit for each other’s work. In some cases, top recruiters could effectively double-dip on work that their subordinates had done. "When you recruit somebody, you can claim up to $250,000 of what they raise," Li said. "In fact, you could poach other people's donors and move money around. And that is how some people reach like $10 million without actually raising a thing. It's like accounting gimmicks and machinations rather than real money. I know there were people who were double counted." As a top fundraiser for both Biden and Harris, Li worked closely with top donors, high-profile members of the party and the Democratic National Committee (DNC). Li described how she had a front-row seat for many of the party’s spending decisions. Li recounted that most of the Harris campaign's spending went through four large media contracting companies. These contractors, Li said, collected enormous fees and received over half a billion dollars. The companies that were listed in her book included Media Buying & Analytics, Gambit Strategies, Bully Pulpit Interactive and Dupont Circle Strategies. CARVILLE SHREDS DEMS' 2024 AUTOPSY, SAYS HARRIS CAMPAIGN WAS 'MOST INEFFECTIVE $2 BILLION EVER SPENT' "This tsunami of money represented about 70 percent of the campaign’s expenditures in the final days, enriching a handful of well-connected consultants while the broader effort collapsed," Li wrote. In interviews with Fox, Li described how the payments to the firms came partially as off-the-top fees. "The vast majority of the money raised went into TV ads. And so... You know, people talk about 10% for the big guy. Okay, but I actually think the bigger grift is 15% for the big grift for these media people. They get 15%, 15 points off of hundreds of millions of dollars. You can do the math," Li said. "The consultants get the money, the consultants that are hired by the campaign, and they're friends of the candidate or friends of Jen O’Malley-Dillon. It's a very incestuous process," Li said, referring to the Harris campaign chair. In addition to the media companies and the lucrative contracts they paid out, Li believes that the party focused too much on expenses that didn’t advance the campaign while, in her view, neglecting strategic opportunities. "$350,000 a night slapping her face in the Las Vegas sphere, spending that money on Gulfstream so they wouldn't have to fly commercial, spending it on Ritz-Carlton hotels. I mean, that definitely happened because the National Finance Committee was hosting its final meeting there. Spending its money on tote bags," Li said. "None of that in Philadelphia," she added, referring to the critical electoral center in Pennsylvania — a state that had been projected to be a pathway to victory in 2024. HARRIS BACKS RELEASING DNC'S 2024 ELECTION AUTOPSY DESPITE LEADERSHIP BURYING REPORT Part of what shocked Li was how brazen the party had been with the money she helped raise. She also expressed disbelief at the message the party spun to voters who had contributed their earnings in hopes of "saving democracy," a refrain Biden used to convince voters to side with him over President Donald Trump. "Some people forked over their life savings. Like people were liquidating their savings on the hope that they were saving the country. They absolutely did, and I truly believe that they donated $2.5 billion over seven weeks, not so much primarily because of Kamala's strength as a candidate, but rather their hatred for Trump and their fear of Trump," Li said. news.title: Rahm Emanuel touts what separates himself from other Dems as he mulls 2028 presidential bid
news.text: AUSTIN, Texas — Former U.S. Ambassador Rahm Emanuel hasn't been shy about his potential prospects for the White House, but as 2028 approaches, the hypothetical Democratic field continues to get more crowded. In an interview with Fox News Digital at the Texas Tribune Festival, Emanuel pointed to three things that separate him from the pack — if he chooses to run. "Candor, authenticity and strength," Emanuel told Fox News Digital. RAHM EMANUEL SPARS WITH NEW YORKER INTERVIEWER WHO GRILLED HIM FOR NOT EMPHASIZING TRANS ISSUES Emanuel's resume in Democratic politics is quite extensive, from serving as a top advisor for Presidents Bill Clinton and Barack Obama, to a congressman, to the mayor of Chicago to, more recently, serving as America's top diplomat in Japan under the Biden administration. If elected president, he insists he "knows what to do on day one." "I'm not gonna tell you what you'd like to hear. We don't have a person to waste or a community to overlook and make the investments that make this country stronger." "And so I'm gonna be honest about it. And I think I bring a level of experience at multiple levels of government that actually, on day one, you start getting the job done. Because we don't have a day to waste," he added.
